    Synonyms: Buchse

Etymology: Inherited from Middle High German bühse. Doublet of Buchse (the Upper German form).

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong tub, vat (fairly large, open vessel)

    Synonyms: Kübel, Pott, Topf, Schüssel, Wanne, Bütte, Zuber

Etymology: From Middle High German botech, boteche, Old High German botega, potacha (“large barrel”) (9th century). Primarily Upper German, likely loaned from a Late Latin variant of apothēca (“storage room, wine cellar”), in Middle Latin also "barrel, vessel, container", making it a doublet of Apotheke, Bodega, and Boutique, or from Latin butica, Late Latin buttis (“barrel”). The Old High German word was feminine, the masculine genus appears in Middle High German, although some Upper German dialects retain feminine gender (Bavarian bottig f).

column8:
noun
  1. masculine, strong custom
    • Bei uns ist es Brauch, die Braut über die Schwelle zu tragen. — Here it is a custom to carry the bride over the threshold.

Etymology: From Middle High German brūch, from Old High German brūh (“use”, noun), ultimately from the root of brauchen (“to need”).

column4:
noun
  1. feminine eyebrow

Etymology: From Middle High German brā (inflected brāw-; rarely also brāwe), from Old High German brāwa (late also brā), from Proto-West Germanic *brāwu, from Proto-Germanic *brēwō. Cognate with Dutch brauw, English brow.

column5:
noun
  1. feminine fizzy pop, soda pop
  2. feminine shower, shower bath, douche, spray

    Synonyms: Dusche

  3. feminine rose (of a watering can or shower head)
  4. feminine effervescence
  5. feminine fermentation

Etymology: Deverbal from brausen (“to whoosh, to roar”).

column7:
noun
  1. masculine, strong mash; mush; porridge; any semisolid food
  2. masculine, strong milk pudding with chewable pieces in it, such as rice pudding, semolina pudding, etc.

    Synonyms: Pudding

Etymology: From Middle High German brīe, brī, from Old High German brīo, from Proto-West Germanic *brīw. Cognate with Yiddish ברײַ (bray).

column5:
noun
  1. feminine breadth, width
  2. feminine latitude
    • Tiere, die in rauem Klima leben, sind oft klüger als ihre Artgenossen aus gemäßigten Breiten, das legen verschiedene Studien nahe. — Animals that live in a rough climate are often smarter than members of the same species from moderate latitudes, that is suggested by different studies.

    Synonyms: Breitengrad, geographische Breite

Etymology: From Middle High German breite, from Old High German breitī, from Proto-Germanic *braidį̄. Analysable as breit + -e. Compare English breadth.

name
  1. feminine, masculine, proper-noun, surname a surname

Etymology: From Middle High German breite, from Old High German breitī, from Proto-Germanic *braidį̄. Analysable as breit + -e. Compare English breadth.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine brake, device for causing deceleration
  2. archaic, feminine any kind of clamp that restricts movement
  3. archaic, feminine any kind of clamp that restricts movement; in particular, a twitch wherewith particularly in veterinary medicine body parts of a beast (face, testicles etc.) are pinched to perform surgical or similar operations

    Synonyms: Kluppe

Etymology: From Middle High German bremse, borrowed from Middle Low German premese (“twitch for horses”), from the verb pramen (“to clamp”), with further origin unclear (DWDS).

noun
  1. feminine horsefly, breezefly, gadfly (fly of the family Tabanidae)

Etymology: From Middle Low German brēmse, borrowed from Old Saxon *brimissa, from *brummōn, from Proto-West Germanic *brummōn (“to buzz, drone”). This form superseded High German Breme (now archaic), from Middle High German breme, from Old High German brema. The form brimissa did exist in Old High German, but both the phonetic development and the attestations prove that it is not the direct source of the modern word.

column8:
noun
  1. masculine, strong piece (part of a larger whole)

Etymology: From Old High German brocco, from Proto-Germanic *brukkô, related to *brukiz.

column4:
name
  1. masculine, proper-noun, strong a mountain in the Harz mountain range, Germany

    Synonyms: Blocksberg

Etymology: Probably from brocken, referring to the mountain's erosion. More at Brocken.

noun
  1. feminine broth
  2. colloquial, derogatory, feminine thin tea or coffee
  3. derogatory, feminine polluted water or liquid

Etymology: From Middle High German brüeje, from Proto-Germanic *brōaną, whence brauen. Related to brühen.

column13:
noun
  1. masculine, strong well, fountain

    Synonyms: Born, Pütz

Etymology: From Middle High German brunne, from Old High German brunno, from Proto-West Germanic *brunnō, from Proto-Germanic *brunnô, whence also Old English burna, Old Norse brunnr; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrun- (“a bubbling forth; a fountain, wellspring, source”). The form is Upper German, most Low and Central German dialects using Born (now poetic in the standard language). This southern origin also explains the vocalism; the expected form is Bronnen with -u- → -o- before a nasal geminate.

column5:
noun
  1. feminine heat, rut (sexual excitement of animals)

    Synonyms: Brunft

  2. feminine sexual arousal

Etymology: From Middle High German brunst, from Old High German brunst, from Proto-Germanic *brunstiz.

noun
  1. feminine bay; gulf; bight

    Synonyms: Golf, Meerbusen

  2. feminine niche, especially one that is wide rather than deep; a slight recess

    Synonyms: Nische

Etymology: 17th century, from Low German, from Middle Low German bucht, from Old Saxon buht, from Proto-West Germanic *buhti, from Proto-Germanic *buhtiz. Cognate with Dutch bocht, English bight.

column3:
noun
  1. feminine, no-plural brownness, the quality of being brown
    • Die Bräune des Holzes gibt dem Raum eine düstere Erscheinung. — The brownness of the wood gives the room a sombre appearance.
    • Der Whisky hat eine tiefe Bräune. — The whisky has a deep brown colour.
  2. feminine, no-plural tan
    • Nach den sonnigen Tagen hatte sie eine gesunde Bräune. — After the sunny days she had a healthy tan.
  3. dated, feminine, no-plural quinsy, croup
    • Und wieder tauchte vor ihrem geistigen Blick eine schreckliche Erinnerung auf, die unaufhörlich auf ihrem Mutterherzen lastete, die Erinnerung an den Tod des letzten Kindchens, das als Säugling an der Bräune gestorben war, und an sein Begräbnis: […].

Etymology: From Middle High German briune (“brownness”); equivalent to braun + -e (“-ness”).

column7:
noun
  1. masculine, strong bridegroom (a man with regard to his wedding)

Etymology: From Middle High German briutegome, from Old High German brūtigomo, from Proto-Germanic *brūdigumô (“bride's man”), from *brūdiz (“bride”) + *gumô (“man”). The modern -i- (from Middle High German -e-) is due to palatisation before -g-, which has been pronounced as a fricative in many dialects. The -a- is a northern variant first attested in Middle Low German brǖdegam and northern Middle High German brūdegame. Further cognate with Dutch bruidegom, English bridegroom, Danish brudgom. Compare also Kashubian brutman (literally “brideman”).

column8:
noun
  1. masculine, strong embankment
  2. masculine, strong perineum

    Synonyms: Perineum

Etymology: From Middle High German tamm. Probably via Old High German *tamm from Proto-West Germanic *damm, from Proto-Germanic *dammaz, though it is sometimes considered a later back-formation from the verb dämmen. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dam).

column9:
noun
  1. masculine, strong steam
  2. masculine, strong vapor / vapour

Etymology: From Middle High German dampf, tampf, from Old High German thamph, damph, tamph, from Proto-Germanic *dampaz. Given the predominant d- in Old High German and quite frequent attestations with th- in related words, the underlying form in High German is probably *þampaz; also attested in the Old Saxon verb thempian. The origin of this byform seems unclear. Eventually derived from Proto-Germanic *dimpaną (“to steam; vaporise”).

noun
  1. masculine, strong intestine, gut

Etymology: From Middle High German darm, from Old High German darm, from Proto-West Germanic *þarm, from Proto-Germanic *þarmaz. Cognate with Old Norse þarmr (whence Danish tarm), obsolete English tharms (“twisted guts”). Compare Ancient Greek τόρμος (tórmos, “hole”).

column4:
noun
  1. feminine date (fruit; tree)

Etymology: From Middle High German datel, dactel, from Old High German dahtil, from Latin dactylus, from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, literally “finger”), a folk-etymological alteration of a Semitic word; compare Hebrew דֶּקֶל (deqel). First attested in the 11th century CE form dahtilboum (“date tree”).

noun
  1. countable, feminine duration
    • Die Dauer des Verfahrens – zwei Monate – hat uns überrascht. — The duration of the process—two months—surprised us.
    • Man kann sagen, daß sich ‚das‘ Mittelalter in den Augen der Musikhistoriker des 19. Jahrhunderts als ein Komplex aus Schichten zusammensetzt, die unterschiedliche Dauern besaßen. — ‘The’ Middle Ages can be said to have consisted in the eyes of 19th-century music historians of a complex of levels that had various durations.
  2. feminine, uncountable permanence
    • Der Friede ist vermutlich nicht von Dauer. — Peace is probably not permanent.

Etymology: Back-formation from dauern.

column56:
verb
  1. transitive, weak to last, to continue, to persist (for a period of time)
    • Der Film dauert zwei Stunden. — The movie lasts two hours.
  2. intransitive, weak to last, to be permanent
    • Unsere Liebe wird dauern. — Our love will last.
  3. impersonal, weak to take time, to take a while
    • Es dauert, bis die Medizin wirkt. — It takes time for the medicine to work.

Etymology: From Middle High German dūren, borrowed from Middle Low German dūren, itself from Latin dūrō. Compare Dutch duren, English dure.

verb
  1. archaic, weak to grieve; to arouse pity; to feel sorry for
    • Aber nachdem ich nun mit dir gesprochen habe, sehe ich als Frau doch noch etwas anderes; ich sehe deine Leiden, und ich kann dir gar nicht ausdrücken, wie sehr du mich dauerst! — I felt sorry for him, but after talking to you, I see it, as a woman, quite differently. I see your agony, and I can't tell you how sorry I am for you!

    Synonyms: leidtun, schmerzen

Etymology: See bedauern.

column5:
noun
  1. masculine, strong rapier, smallsword
  2. masculine, strong épée
  3. masculine, obsolete, strong dagger

Etymology: Since ca. 1400, at first as degen, but also dege, dägen, tägen. Usually derived from Middle French dague, but the origin of the e-vocalism is unclear. An eastern dialectal *degue is possible, but apparently unattested, whereas Czech dýka is considered a borrowing from German. See French dague and Italian daga for more. Probably also related with the family of English dagger. From the 17th century, the sense “dagger” is restricted to Dolch, while Degen comes to refer to longer weapons, especially thrust-oriented dueling swords. By the 18th century it was used of any sword worn as part of a uniform.

noun
  1. archaic, masculine, poetic, strong hero, warrior, soldier
    • [Der Prinz.] […] Er war es, der sich meinen Ansprüchen auf Sabionetta am meisten widersetzte. – Ein alter Degen; stolz und rauh; sonst bieder und gut! — It was him who opposed my demands to Sabionetta the most. - An old warrior; proud and gruff; otherwise trustworthy and good!
    • [Thibaut.] Wo aber waren denn die tapfern Degen / Saintrailles, La Hire und Frankreichs Brustwehr, / Der heldenmütge Bastard, daß der Feind / So allgewaltig reißend vorwärts drang? — But where were then those brave heroes: Saintrailles, La Hire and France's bulwark, the heroic bastard, that the enemy thrust forward so overwhelmingly, rapaciously?

Etymology: From Middle High German dëgen, from Old High German dëgan. Cognate with Dutch degen, English thane, Icelandic þegn, Ancient Greek τέκνον (téknon). The word had become archaic by 1500, but was revived in poetic style since the later 18th century. This use may be a learned borrowing from Middle High German as there appear to be no attestations between ca. 1650 and 1750.

column7:
noun
  1. masculine, strong dyke, dike; permanent dam
    • Wenn der Deich bricht, wird das ganze Tal überflutet. — If the dike breaks, the whole valley will be flooded.
    • Zwölf Boxkämpfer jagen Viktor quer über den großen Sylter Deich. — Twelve boxers chase Viktor across the big Sylt dike.

Etymology: From Middle Low German dīk, from Old Saxon dīk, from Proto-West Germanic *dīk, from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz. Originally the same word as Teich (“pond”). The sense “dike” spread via Low German, for which reason the form Deich is most often regarded as an artificial adaptation of Middle Low German dīk (“dike”) to the phonetic system of standard German. However, Deich is also the form natively developed in West Central German and it does mean “dike, dam, weir system” in most dialects of the Rhineland, particularly along the Lower Rhine. The supposition of an artificial adaptation is therefore possible but not inevitable. Cognate to Dutch dijk, to West Frisian dyk, to English dyke, dike and to Saterland Frisian Diek.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine carriage pole, pole, shaft, drawbar
  2. feminine pall

Etymology: From Middle High German dīhsel, from Old High German dīhsala, from Proto-West Germanic *þīhslu, from Proto-Germanic *þinhslō.

noun
  1. alt-of, dated, feminine dated form of Dechsel (“adze”)

Etymology: Etymology 1 above yielded Dechsel or Dichsel in several dialects through shortening before the consonant cluster. The words thus merged and the fuller (thus seemingly more correct) form Deichsel was generalised. Compare Dutch dissel (both “adze” and “drawbar”).

noun
  1. feminine dent
    • Nach dem Unfall hatte ich eine tiefe Delle in der Motorhaube. — After the accident I had a deep dent in my car’s bonnet.
  2. feminine hollow

Etymology: From Middle High German telle, from Old High German *tella, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *daljō. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German delle). The form Tell(e) persists dialectally. Cognate with Dutch (dialectal) del and English dell.

column3:
noun
  1. feminine, no-plural humility, meekness (comprehension or expression of one’s own lowliness)

    Synonyms: Bescheidenheit, Ergebenheit, Unterwürfigkeit

Etymology: From Middle High German dēmuot, diemuot, diemüete, from southern Old High German thiomuotī (ca. 800), from thio (“unfree, adscript”) + muot (“mood, attitude”), thus literally “serf-mindedness”. The word spread from Upper German during Middle High German times, gradually displacing the northern ōtmuotī (compare Old Saxon ōthmōdī). Northern sources almost invariably show -e- instead of -ie-, but this form also appears in the south and must thus be considered an internal, irregular development. Middle Low German dêmôt, Middle Dutch dêmoet are both late (15th c.) borrowings from High German.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine, plural-normally plank (most often on a floor)
    • Du hörst mich nachts / Über Dielen gehn / Ich laufe hier wie irr herum / Und rauch die zehnte Zigarette / Innerhalb der halben Stunde / Die mir bleibt / Bis mich das Licht vertreibt
  2. Germany, feminine hallway, hall, foyer (room)

    Synonyms: Flur, Gang, Korridor, Vorzimmer

Etymology: From Middle High German dille, from Old High German dilla, from Proto-Germanic *þiljǭ. More at thill. The sense “hallway” is from Middle Low German dēle and its German Low German descendants. The form, Diele, likewise seems influenced by Low German (although it could stem from an attested Middle High German variant dile). Cognate with Dutch deel f.

column7:
noun
  1. masculine, strong service
    • ausgezeichneter Dienst — excellent service
  2. masculine, strong work, duty

Etymology: From Middle High German dienst, dienest, from Old High German dionest, dionōst, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz. Compare the Old English þēonest, þēnest. See also German dienen.

column5:
noun
  1. also, dated, derogatory, feminine whore (prostitute or sexually unreserved woman)
    • Der, nach dem Schauspiel, hofft ein Kartenspiel, / Der eine wilde Nacht an einer Dirne Busen. — One, after the play, hopes for a card game / another, for a wild night on the bosom of a harlot.
    • Das Glück ist eine leichte Dirne, / Und weilt nicht gern am selben Ort; / Sie streicht das Haar dir von der Stirne / Und küßt dich rasch und flattert fort. — Luck is an easy girl / And does not like to linger in a place; / She wipes your hair from your brow / And kisses you swiftly and flutters away.

    Synonyms: Buhldirne, Hure, Lustdirne, Nutte, Dirne, Flittchen, Freudenmädchen, Hübschlerin, Liebedienerin, Liebesdienerin, Metze, Nudelschnecke, Prostituierte, Sexarbeiterin

  2. archaic, dialectal, feminine girl; lass

Etymology: From Middle High German dierne (“girl; servant”), from Old High German diorna, thiorna (“girl; servant”), from Proto-West Germanic *þewernā. Doublet of Deern. The sense “prostitute” developed from the use for a “girl from the lower classes”. It is first attested in the 15th century.

column7:
noun
  1. masculine, strong wick (porous cord that draws up liquid fuel for burning)

Etymology: From Middle High German tāht, from Old High German tāht, from Proto-Germanic *þanhtu-/*þæhta- (“thread”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *tek- (“to weave”). Cognate with Old Norse þáttr, for which reason the onset t- is an irregular hardening (compare tausend). The modern form is not inherited from literary Middle High German, but from the vernaculars. It has d- due to dialectal High German, and Low German influence (compare Middle Low German dacht); the vocalism is due to the common dialectal development -ā- → -ō- (compare Odem).

column8:
noun
  1. masculine, strong cod (marine fish of the family Gadidae)

Etymology: From Middle High German dorsch, borrowed from Middle Low German dorsch, itself from Old Norse þorskr, from Proto-Germanic *þurskaz.

column5:
noun
  1. masculine, neuter, strong yolk

    Synonyms: Eigelb, Eidotter

Etymology: From Middle High German toter, tuter, from Old High German totoro, tutaro, from Proto-West Germanic *dodrō. The modern form with initial d- and internal -tt- is of dialectal, probably Bavarian, origin.

noun
  1. masculine, strong dodder (Cuscuta gen. et spp. and Camelina gen. et spp.)

    Synonyms: Seide

Etymology: From Middle High German toter, tother, from Old High German totir, from Proto-West Germanic *dodr.

column8:
noun
  1. masculine, strong pressure; stress
  2. figuratively, masculine, strong urge; impulse; longing
    • Humanismus soll eine geistige Bewegung sein, die in einem Drang nach Wiederbelebung des klassischen Altertums wurzelt. — Humanism shall be a spiritual movement that is rooted in an urge for the revival of the classical antiquity.

Etymology: Akin to the verb dringen (“to press”). From Proto-Germanic *þrangwaz (“pressing, narrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat; pound; hew; press”). Cognate with English throng and Dutch drang.

column92:
verb
  1. class-3, intransitive, strong to insist; to press
    • auf etwas dringen — to press for something / to insist on something
  2. class-3, intransitive, strong to ooze; to seep
    • in etwas dringen — to seep into something
  3. class-3, intransitive, strong to penetrate, to force one’s way
    • durch etwas dringen — to penetrate something

Etymology: From Middle High German dringen, from Old High German dringan. Akin to drängen and Drang. Cognate with dialectal English thring and, more distantly, with English throng.

column9:
noun
  1. masculine, strong aroma, fragrance
    • Er bemerkte einen süßlichen Duft als er die Küche betrat. — He noticed a sweet aroma as he entered the kitchen.

Etymology: From Middle High German tuft, from Old High German duft, thuft, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, be obscured”) (DWDS); cognate with Danish duft (“fragrance”) and possibly Ancient Greek τῠφλός (tŭphlós, “blind”). The Middle High German t- is an irregular hardening (compare tausend) that was undone in modern German.

column8:
noun
  1. masculine, strong haze, mist

Etymology: From Middle High German dunst, tunst, from Old High German tunst, from Proto-Germanic *dunstą (“haze, mist, dust, evaporation”). Related to English dust. The onset d- is already predominant in Middle High German, thus due to irregular re-voicing. The expected form tunst disappears in early modern German under the reinforcing influence of Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dūst, from Old Saxon thunst).

column3:
adv
  1. Austria, Switzerland, dated, especially, regional back
    • Bei ihnen reisen jedoch die Vermögenden wie die Windsbraut durch ganz Italien und wieder retour, haben Italien und nichts von der Welt gesehen, und ein anderes Mal fahren sie mit derselben Eile nach Paris, sehen mit diebischer Freude alle Cafés chantants und wissen viel von den Boulevards, aber nichts von den Franzosen.
    • Wie komm’ ich dazu, daß ich mich soll zwei Tage im Hotel mopsen und dann gleich wieder retour, bloß wegen –.

    Synonyms: zurück

Etymology: Borrowed from French retour.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine ebb, low tide

Etymology: 16th century, from Middle Low German ebbe, from Old Saxon *ebbia, from Proto-West Germanic *abbjā, from Proto-Germanic *abjǭ. Cognate to Dutch eb, English ebb.

column5:
noun
  1. feminine marriage (state of being married; life as a married couple)

Etymology: From Middle High German ē, ēwe, from Old High German ēwa, from Proto-West Germanic *aiw, from Proto-Germanic *aiwǭ, *aiwaz (“law, custom”).

column6:
noun
  1. feminine honour
    • zu seinen Ehren — in his honour [grammatically plural in original]
  2. feminine credit
  3. feminine kudos

Etymology: From Middle High German ēre, from Old High German ēra (“honour, fame, sense of honour”), from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀu, from Proto-Germanic *aizō. Cognate with Old Norse eir (“pardon, gentleness”), Old Saxon ēra (“honour, protection, pardon, gift”), Old English ār (“honour, help, pardon”), and Latin aes-tumare (“to acknowledge, value”).

column5:
noun
  1. feminine A small lizard, especially of the Lacertidae family.
  2. feminine Lacerta (astronomical constellation)

Etymology: From Middle High German eidehse, egdehse, egedehse, from Old High German egidehsa (“lizard”).

noun
  1. feminine, no-plural hurry

Etymology: From Middle High German īlaé, from Old High German īla, from Proto-West Germanic *īlu, from Proto-Germanic *īlō (“rush, haste”).

column6:
noun
  1. Germany, masculine, strong bucket, pail

    Synonyms: Kübel

  2. colloquial, derogatory, masculine, strong idiot, loser

Etymology: From Middle High German eim(b)er, einber, Old High German einber, from Proto-West Germanic *ambrī. Cognate with Luxembourgish Eemer.

column5:
name
  1. feminine, masculine, proper-noun, surname a surname

Etymology: From the ancient Germanic personal name *Agimar, composed of *aggju (“point, edge (of a sword)”) + *mārī (“famous”).

noun
  1. masculine, no-plural, strong disgust, loathing

Etymology: From Middle Low German ēkel, probably from the verb in German ekeln, which see.

column6:
noun
  1. informal, neuter, strong a mean or repulsive person

Etymology: From Middle Low German ēkel, probably from the verb in German ekeln, which see.

column4:
noun
  1. neuter, no-plural, strong misery
    • Das religiöse Elend ist in einem der Ausdruck des wirklichen Elendes und in einem die Protestation gegen das wirkliche Elend. — Religious suffering is, at one and the same time, the expression of real suffering and a protest against real suffering.
    • Das Elend der Universitäten beginnt, wie wir sahen, schon bei den Grundschulen und High Schools. — The misery of the universities begins, as we have seen, already in the primary schools and high schools.

Etymology: From elend.

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong elbow

Etymology: From Middle High German elenboge, from Old High German elinbogo, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô; by surface analysis, Elle + Bogen.

column5:
noun
  1. masculine, strong oriel; bay (on houses)

Etymology: From Middle High German ärkēr (in rhyme with mēr), ärker or ærker (in rhyme with der), ultimately from Latin arcus.

noun
  1. feminine harvest

Etymology: From Middle High German erne f (alongside arn m), from Old High German arn f, from Proto-Germanic *azaniz f. Cognate with Middle Dutch arn, Middle Low German erne, arne, Old English *ern (in rugern). The modern form with an alveolar plosive (first attested in Middle High German ernde f) stems from merger with related Old High German arnōt m, from Proto-Germanic *azanōdaz.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine ash (tree)

Etymology: From Middle High German esche f, asch m, from Old High German asca f, asc m, from Proto-West Germanic *ask. The umlaut can be explained here from the plural of the masculine noun, though it may also be due to the secondary umlaut triggered by following -sch- which is found throughout western dialects of High German (compare Äsche, where this is probably the cause of the umlaut).

name
  1. neuter, proper-noun Eš (a village in the Czech Republic)

Etymology: From Middle High German esche f, asch m, from Old High German asca f, asc m, from Proto-West Germanic *ask. The umlaut can be explained here from the plural of the masculine noun, though it may also be due to the secondary umlaut triggered by following -sch- which is found throughout western dialects of High German (compare Äsche, where this is probably the cause of the umlaut).

column10:
noun
  1. masculine, strong ass, donkey
  2. figuratively, masculine, strong a stupid person
  3. figuratively, masculine, strong a stubborn person

Etymology: From Middle High German esel, from Old High German esil, from late Proto-West Germanic *asil, which is borrowed from Late Latin asellus.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine school (an institution dedicated to teaching and learning (especially before university); department/institute at a college or university; art movement; followers of a particular doctrine)
    • Ab Morgen haben wir wieder Schule. — Starting tomorrow/from tomorrow onwards we will have school again.

Etymology: Attested from the 15th century, in the 14th in the compound götzenträger for "icon". In the 15th and 16th centuries a term for "cast image", and more generally for "image, likeness". In the 15th century used in the sense of "fool, stupid person", presumably influenced by Götz, a short form of the given name Gottfried. Grimm cites a folk song collected by Uhland (1881), based on a manuscript dated to 1603, where götze takes the meaning of kobold as evidence that this may have been the original sense. The meaning of "false god, idol" is due to Luther. Early usage in Luther is in the sense of "mask" or "mummer", especially of clerics as the "masks" of the pope, or the pope as "mask" of the devil; later, Luther moves away from this usage and begins using the word as a synonym of Abgott "false god".

Cognates outside Germanic only in Latvian sermulis and Lithuanian šarmuõ, šermuõ. The monophthong -i- in modern German (alongside obsolete Hermlein, Hermelein) as well as the final stress can be explained natively, as being from a non-diphthongising dialect on the one hand, and by comparing the irregular stress shift in such words as Holunder, Wacholder, lebendig on the other. However, it seems likely that both developments were reinforced by Romance words such as Italian ermellino, armellino, French hermine. Etymology: From Middle High German kegel, from Old High German chegil, kegil (“peg”), especially pegs for a tent (zeltchegil) or similar. Middle High German kegel means “peg or pin used for a game” (such as skittles), but regional use from the 14th century onward also preserve a more general meaning of “peg, cudgel”. The etymology cannot be traced with certainty. The word is a member of a Wortsippe which also includes Keil (“wedge”), German Kugel (“ball, sphere”) and Kiel (“keel”). No cognates of Kegel are known outside of German (other than loans from German in Dutch, Scandinavian as well as Baltic and Slavic languages). French quille seems to be a reflex of an Old Frankish form of the word. Proto-Slavic *žezlъ (“stick, staff, rod”) has diverse proposed origins. The German word Keil (“wedge”) is closely related, compared by Grimm to the relationship of Latin cuneus (“wedge”) with cōnus (“cone”). In some dialects, Keil was used as the term for both “wedge” and “bowling pin”. On the other hand, Kroonen suggests a derivation from Proto-Germanic *kagilaz (“cone, pin”), from the root underlying Proto-Germanic *kagô (“trunk”) + *-ilaz (“diminutive suffix, agent suffix”). Also closely related is Kugel (“ball, sphere”). All these terms developed in context of the game of skittles. The relation of Keil to Kegel (both terms for the pin) was the same as that of Kaule to Kugel (both terms for the ball; the former remained dialectal, while Kugel became the generic term for "sphere"). For the development of the sense of an illegitimate son compare German Bengel, Flegel, Balg and the like.

The form with -f- is an adaptation to the High German consonantism, for which there may have been rare antetypes in northern dialects of Central German, but which was chiefly artificial. Kneipen remained predominant until the earlier 19th century, but was somewhat informal. The more standard-looking kneifen then fully established itself in written German and displaced kneipen by the mid-20th century.

Etymology: From Middle High German knote, knode, from Old High German knoto, knodo. The two forms are probably variants based on Grammatischer Wechsel. The form with -t- (from Proto-Germanic *-d-) was predominant in East Central German, that with -d- (from Proto-Germanic *-þ-) in Upper German. Incidentally, this situation explains the lengthened vowel in the standardized form (lengthening being blocked before -t- in Upper German, but not in Central German). Neither German form can be derived directly from Proto-Germanic *knuttô, whence Middle High German knotze and English knot, though a relation is very likely. The senses “journeyman”, “person (of some quality)” are probably due, at least in part, to conflation with Middle Low German genôte (“mate, companion”), cognate of German Genosse. Alongside, there is a common tendency of referring to people, especially children, with words for thick, plump, or inflated objects (compare e.g. Balg).

Probably the dissimilated variant körpel received the umlaut by analogy with diminutives in -el. Some Central German dialects show secondary umlaut before -r- + labial (see Hunsrik Kerrper, Kerrver and Luxembourgish Kierper), but precisely these dialects make little or no use of this word. Immediate cognates are Middle Dutch croech, Old English crōg, of obscure origin. Possibly from a Proto-Indo-European root shared with Old Armenian կարաս (karas, “pitcher, large jar”), Ancient Greek κρωσσός (krōssós, “pitcher”), but the phonetics are problematic. Also compare Old Irish croiccenn (“skin”). The originally Low German Kruke (“crock”), cognate with English crock, is another word, though a relation with Krug is considered likely.

column5:
noun
  1. neuter, strong, uncountable life; being alive; a state in which organic entities such as animals, plants and bacteria have properties like metabolism, adaptation and replication
    • Das Leben ist nicht an das geistige Bewusstsein gebunden. — Life is not dependent on mental consciousness.
  2. neuter, strong, uncountable life; being alive; the entirety of those who are in this state
    • Die Erde quillt über vor Leben. — Earth is full of life.
  3. countable, neuter, strong life; being alive; the time period in which one is in this state; the time between birth and death
    • Das Leben beginnt mit der Geburt und endet mit dem Tod. — Life begins with birth and ends with death.

    • Nicht jeder, der atmet, ist auch wirklich am Leben. — Not everyone who breathes is really alive.

    • Das Leben der Edelgard. — The life of Edelgard.
    • Sein Leben weist viele Höhen und Tiefen auf. — There are many ups and downs in his biography.

    Synonyms: Biographie, Lebenslauf, Vita

  7. neuter, strong, uncountable, usually existence; life (a position one has created for oneself, often manifested in success, prosperity, and standing)
    • Frau Schmidt hat sich in all diesen Jahren ein bewundernswertes Leben aufgebaut. — Mrs Schmidt has built up an admirable life in all these years.

    • Du hast nur noch drei Leben übrig. — You only have three lives left.

Upper German synonyms were Old High German rātisca, rātissa, rātunga.

    • Das rätst du nie. — You will never guess that.

Etymology: From Middle High German rāten, from Old High German rātan, from Proto-West Germanic *rādan, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaną. Cognate with Low German raden, Dutch raden, English rede, read, Danish råde.

    • Aufgrund einer Bombendrohung musste das Gebäude geräumt werden. — Due to a bomb threat, the building had to be evacuated.

Probably from the same ultimate source as English plug. Further origin uncertain. The word shows semantic relations with a nominal derivative of Proto-Germanic *plukkijaną (“to pluck”, phlucke, phlocke, pluck, plok), and at least in High German also with the descendant of *blukką (“block”). However, these relations are in all likelihood secondary. Within High German, the word appears to have been restricted chiefly to the north-east (East Central German and surroundings); therefore it has been argued to be a Low German borrowing in the colonial regions, but the late attestations in all languages make it hard to prove this. English plug and similar Scandinavian forms are usually considered borrowings.

column9:
noun
  1. masculine, strong trunk; torso (body excluding the head and limbs)
  2. masculine, strong hull (clipping of Schiffsrumpf)
    • Kapitän! Eine Katastrophe! Wir müssen dringend dem Notruf absetzen! Wir haben ein riesiges Loch im Rumpf!
  3. masculine, strong fuselage (clipping of Flugzeugrumpf)

Etymology: From Middle High German rumph, perhaps ultimately related to rümpfen (“to wrinkle”). See English rump for more.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine wrinkle

Etymology: From Middle High German runzel, from Old High German runzula, runzila, a diminutive of Proto-West Germanic *hrunkwitā (“wrinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreng-, from a nasalized form of Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerg-, from a phonetic extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). Compare Old Norse hrukka (“wrinkle”), Swedish rynka (“wrinkle”).

column51:
verb
  1. weak to equip, to arm
  2. Switzerland, transitive, weak to prepare, make ready
    • einen Salat rüsten — to prepare a salad

    Synonyms: anrichten, vorbereiten

Etymology: From Middle High German rüsten, from Old High German rusten, hrusten (“prepare, adorn”) (8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *hrustijan, cognate with Old English hyrstan (“equip, adorn”), root-cognate with Greek κρύπτω (krúptō, “cover, conceal”).

column54:
verb
  1. intransitive, transitive, weak to sow
    • Wer Hass sät, wird Hass ernten. — He who sows hatred will reap hate.

Etymology: From Middle High German sæjen, from Old High German sāen, sājen, sāwen, from Proto-West Germanic *sāan, from Proto-Germanic *sēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-. Compare Dutch zaaien, English sow, Danish så, Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌹𐌰𐌽 (saian). The expected modern spelling would be with an -h- to mark the hiatus (as in mähen, nähen), but this was avoided to distinguish säen from sähen, subjunctive of sehen (“to see”).

column4:
noun
  1. feminine string (of a musical stringed instrument)
  2. feminine string (of a racquet)

Etymology: From Middle High German seite, from Old High German seita (also seito m), from Proto-West Germanic *saidā, *saidō, from Proto-Germanic *saidô (“string, cord”). In the 17th century, the ⟨ei⟩ was changed to the homophonous ⟨ai⟩, in order to distinguish this word from Seite. Derived from Seite originally.

column9:
noun
  1. masculine, strong velvet

Etymology: Inherited from Middle High German samīt, borrowed from Old French samit, from Medieval Latin samitum, borrowed from Medieval Greek ἑξάμιτος (hexámitos), from Ancient Greek ἑξα- (hexa-, “six”) + μῐ́τος (mĭ́tos, “thread, strand”).

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong saddle
  2. masculine, strong nut of a string instrument (supporting strings at the head end)

    Synonyms: Obersattel

Etymology: From Middle High German satel, from Old High German satal, from Proto-West Germanic *sadul, from Proto-Germanic *sadulaz. Cognate with Old Norse sǫðull, Old English sadol, Dutch zadel, English saddle.

column3:
noun
  1. feminine scraper, flat instrument with a handle used for scraping

    Synonyms: Schaber, Schabeisen

  2. feminine cockroach

    Synonyms: Kakerlake, Küchenschabe

  3. dialectal, feminine, obsolete scabies

    Synonyms: Krätze, Räude

Etymology: From Middle High German schabe (“scraper, chaff, moulding; moth, cockroach”), from Old High German scaba (“scraper, plane”), from Proto-Germanic *skabō (“scraper”). Cognate with Dutch schaaf (“plane”). Also related to German Low German Schabbe (“mange, scabies”), English scab.

column8:
noun
  1. masculine, strong shaft, mineshaft (tunnel)

Etymology: Borrowed from Middle Low German schacht, from Old Saxon skaft, from Proto-West Germanic *skaft. Doublet of Schaft.

noun
  1. masculine, strong shaft (pole)
  2. masculine, strong upper (of a shoe), leg (of a boot)

Etymology: From Middle High German schaft, from Old High German skaft, scaft, from Proto-West Germanic *skaft. Doublet of Schacht.

noun
  1. feminine a small, usually square box, package or case
  2. feminine, obsolete, vulgar vulva, vagina

    Synonyms: Dose

  3. derogatory, feminine woman

Etymology: 15th century, from Italian scatola, with metathesis from Latin castulum, itself a diminutive of Lombardic Old High German kasto. Hence a doublet of inherited Kasten as well as the later borrowing Schatulle. The -ch- is due to a Bavarian consonantal development, for which compare Spachtel.

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong skull
  2. also, figuratively, masculine, strong head
    • Ich seh' tausend Augen, und sie sind geschlossen / Klopf an tausend Türen und keine is' offen / Ich sauf' mich voll bis mir der Schädel dröhnt — I see a thousand eyes, and they're closed / Knock on a thousand doors and none are open / I drink and drink till my head is pounding
  3. colloquial, masculine, strong headache, particularly one due to excessive drinking

    Synonyms: Brummschädel

  4. masculine, slang, strong head
    • Ich bin nicht back, war nie fort, dein Mädel gibt mir Schädel — I'm not back, I was never away, your girlfriend is giving me head
    • Ich muss große Träume leben, krieg' von Rotlichtbräuten Schädel

Etymology: From Middle High German schedel (“skull”). Further origin uncertain. Borrowing from Middle Low German schêdel (“top of the head, head, skull”), cognate with German Scheitel (“top of the head, parting of the hair”), suggests itself, but is not embraced in most of the literature. If that theory is correct, then it would be derived from Proto-West Germanic *skaidilu (“part in the hair, top, crown, crest, summit”).

column7:
noun
  1. masculine, strong shepherd

    Synonyms: Schafhirt

Etymology: From Middle High German schæfære, from late Old High German scāphāre. Equivalent to Schaf (“sheep”) + -er. Compare Dutch schaper, scheper.

column6:
name
  1. feminine, masculine, proper-noun, surname a surname originating as an occupation, equivalent to English Shepherd

Etymology: From Middle High German schæfære, from late Old High German scāphāre. Equivalent to Schaf (“sheep”) + -er. Compare Dutch schaper, scheper.

noun
  1. masculine, strong conductor (of a bus, tram, train etc)

    Synonyms: Kondukteur, Kundenbetreuer im Nahverkehr, Zugbegleiter

Etymology: From the verb schaffen.

column7:
noun
  1. informal, masculine, no-plural, strong nonsense
    • Was für ein Quatsch ist das? — What kind of nonsense is that?

    Synonyms: Unsinn, Blödsinn, Schwachsinn, Stuss

  2. informal, masculine, no-plural, strong joking, kidding, fun
    • Ich mach doch nur Quatsch. — I’m just joking, you know.
  3. masculine, no-plural, strong chat
    • Ein kleiner Quatsch in der Mittagspause ist doch immer schön. — A little chat during lunchbreak is always nice.

    Synonyms: Unterhaltung, Schwatz, Schwätzchen, Plauderei, Plausch, Schnack

Etymology: Deverbal from quatschen.

column3:
intj
  1. used to acknowledge that the speaker has just misspoken and to introduce the correction
    • Zu Hause habe ich eine Katze, Quatsch, zwei Katzen. — At home I have a cat, I mean, two cats.

Etymology: Deverbal from quatschen.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine swing (seat hanging on two lines)
  2. broadly, feminine any swinging construction, including seesaws and similar devices

Etymology: With -au- by artificial adaptation to standard German from Low German Schukel, a lengthened variant of Low German Schuckel (also early modern German Schuckel), deverbal from schuckeln, schockeln, iterative of Middle Low German and Middle High German schocken, from Proto-West Germanic *skokkōn. Related with English shock.

column9:
noun
  1. feminine shovel

    Synonyms: Schüppe, Schippe

Etymology: From Middle High German schūfele, schūvele, from Old High German scūvala, from Proto-Germanic *skuflō. Cognate with English shovel.

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong citizen (legal member of a state) (male or unspecified)

    Synonyms: Staatsangehöriger

Etymology: From Staat + -s- + Bürger.

column9:
noun
  1. masculine, strong sound

    Synonyms: Ton, Geräusch, Klang, Laut

  2. masculine, strong a resonating sound, one that is either very loud or reverberant

Etymology: From Middle High German schal, from Old High German scal, from Proto-West Germanic *skellan, from Proto-Germanic *skellaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”). Cognate with Dutch schal and Swedish skall. Compare English low (“to moo”).

column4:
noun
  1. feminine, no-plural shame (uncomfortable feeling at one's own impropriety or at the exposure of something private; but not in the sense of disgrace or being dishonored, for which Schande)
  2. feminine, no-plural bashfulness, prudishness, shamefacedness
  3. dated, feminine, no-plural pubic region including the genitals
    • Schamhaar — pubic hair
  4. dated, feminine, no-plural vulva

Etymology: From Middle High German schame, from Old High German scama, from Proto-West Germanic *skamu, from Proto-Germanic *skamō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European [Term?]. Compare Dutch schaamte, English shame, Danish skam.

column5:
noun
  1. feminine troop
  2. feminine family

Etymology: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German scara (“troop”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaru, from Proto-Germanic *skarō. Cognate with English share, Swedish skara.

column8:
noun
  1. feminine, mixed, neuter, strong ploughshare

Etymology: From Middle High German schar, from Old High German scaro. Cognate with German scheren (“to shear”), German Schere (“shear, scissors”), English share (“plowshare”), English shear.

column54:
verb
  1. weak to give as a present, to gift
    • [with accusative ‘something’ and dative ‘someone’]
    • Ich schenke meiner Tochter ein Kätzchen zum Geburtstag. — I’m giving my daughter a kitten for her birthday.

    Synonyms: geben, spendieren, bescheren, verehren, zuwenden, zum Geschenk machen

  2. weak to spare one(self) (something)
    • Joseph hätte sich die beschwerliche weite Reise gern geschenkt, doch er wagte es nicht, ungehorsam zu sein. — Joseph would have gladly spared himself the long, onerous journey, but he didn't dare to be disobedient.

    Synonyms: ersparen

  3. formal, transitive, weak to pour from a vessel, to serve
    • Sie schenkte den Wein in zwei Gläser. — She poured the wine in two glasses.

    Synonyms: schütten, gießen, einschütten, eingießen, einschenken, ausschenken

Etymology: From Middle High German schenken, from Old High German scenken, from Proto-West Germanic *skankijan (“to pour, serve”).

column97:
adj
  1. shy (reserved)

    Synonyms: zurückhaltend, schüchtern

  2. shy, skittish, startlish (easily frightened)
    • scheu wie ein Reh

    Synonyms: schreckhaft

Etymology: From Middle High German schiech, schiehe, schie, schiuch, schiuhe, schūche, from Old High German *skioh, from Proto-West Germanic *skeuh. The modern form goes back to the Central German forms with -iu-, -ū-. These are usually interpreted as alterations based on Scheu (noun) and scheuen (verb), though this does not seem unquestionable in view of Middle Dutch schu, Middle Low German schǖ. The form with -ie- remains in dialectal Upper German schiech (“ugly”). Cognate with Dutch schuw, English shy.

column73:
adj
  1. skew, oblique, askew, leaning, slanting, aslant, inclined (neither parallel nor perpendicular)
  2. slopy, sloping (characterised by a slope or slopes)
  3. crooked, awry (set at an angle; not vertical or square)
  4. lopsided (not even or balanced; not the same on one side as on the other)
  5. wry (turned away, contorted)
  6. distorted (misshapen; brought out of shape)
  7. worn (damaged and shabby as a result of much use)
  8. figuratively inappropriate (not suitable for the situation, time, or place)

Etymology: From northern Middle High German schief, schīf (etc.), from Middle Low German schêf, from Old Saxon *skêf, from Proto-West Germanic *skaib, from Proto-Germanic *skaibaz. Regular High German cognates exist only in north-western Central German; compare Central Franconian scheif, northernmost Luxembourgish scheef. Otherwise it was borrowed from Low German into the colonial dialects, i.e. East Central German, with fallible phonetic interpretation of the original form (hence variously -ie-, -ī-, -ē-, -ei-, -b-, -f-, etc.). The word established itself in standard German during the 18th century. Cognate with Dutch scheef, Old English *sċ(e)āf (in sċāffōt), Old Norse skeifr.

column3:
adv
  1. crookedly, at an angle
  2. lopsidedly
  3. figuratively askance (sideways; obliquely)
  4. badly, wrong (in a way that isn't right)

Etymology: From northern Middle High German schief, schīf (etc.), from Middle Low German schêf, from Old Saxon *skêf, from Proto-West Germanic *skaib, from Proto-Germanic *skaibaz. Regular High German cognates exist only in north-western Central German; compare Central Franconian scheif, northernmost Luxembourgish scheef. Otherwise it was borrowed from Low German into the colonial dialects, i.e. East Central German, with fallible phonetic interpretation of the original form (hence variously -ie-, -ī-, -ē-, -ei-, -b-, -f-, etc.). The word established itself in standard German during the 18th century. Cognate with Dutch scheef, Old English *sċ(e)āf (in sċāffōt), Old Norse skeifr.

column97:
adj
  1. slim, svelte

Etymology: From Middle High German slanc, Middle Low German slank, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *slingwaną (“to twist, wind”), the source of schlingen.

adj
  1. clever in a way that enables one to achieve one's goals; slightly sly or cunning (but not usually implying any evil intentions)

    Synonyms: gewieft, pfiffig, clever, ausgebufft

  2. informal bright, intelligent, clever (with no such overtone at all)

    Synonyms: klug, gescheit, intelligent

Etymology: Borrowed from Middle Low German slû, whence probably also Dutch sluw. Further origin uncertain. Probably from a Proto-Germanic *slūhaz (“sneaking, creeping”), which seems to trace back to a Proto-Indo-European *(s)lewǵ- (“to crawl, slide”) (albeit without any known extra-Germanic cognates), if the original sense referred to sneaking and sliding. Related to Dutch sluiken (“to creep, smuggle, act clandestinely”). In spite of the near-identity in meaning and form, English sly is in all likelihood not related.

column6:
noun
  1. jargon, masculine, neuter, strong scarlet (colour)

    Synonyms: Scharlachrot, Scharlachfarbe

  2. jargon, masculine, neuter, strong scarlet-colored fabric

Etymology: From Middle High German scharlach, backformation from northern Middle High German scharlachen, from Middle Dutch scarlaken, alteration (based on Middle Dutch laken = German Laken) of older *scarlaten (early modern Dutch schaerlaten, southern Middle High German scharlāt), from Old French escarlate, from Persian سقرلاط (saqerlât), from Latin sigillātum.

column4:
noun
  1. masculine, no-plural, strong scarlet fever

Etymology: Clipping of Scharlachfieber, since the first half of the 19th century.

noun
  1. feminine show

Etymology: Inherited from Middle High German schouwe, equivalent to a deverbal from schauen.

column53:
verb
  1. copulative, transitive, weak to watch, to view (a movie or other performance)
    • Ich schaue gern Fußball. — I like to watch football/soccer.
  2. Austria, Bavaria, Southern-Germany, copulative, intransitive, weak to look (at something, at a certain location, in a certain direction, in a certain way)
    • Schau, ich hab die Schlüssel gefunden. — Look, I found the keys.
    • Warum schaust du denn so böse? — Why are you looking so angry?
  3. Austria, Bavaria, Southern-Germany, copulative, intransitive, weak to look (at something, at a certain location, in a certain direction, in a certain way); to look
  4. Austria, Bavaria, Southern-Germany, intransitive, weak to watch out, to take care; to make sure, to see to it
    • Schaut, dass ihr pünktlich seid. — Make sure that you’ll be on time
    • Keine Sorge, ich schau, dass du nicht ins Gefängnis kommst. — Don't worry, I'll see to it that you don't go to jail.

    Synonyms: zusehen

  5. Austria, Bavaria, Southern-Germany, intransitive, weak to look (at); to watch [with auf (+ accusative) or nach (+ dative) ‘someone/something’]; the construction with nach often implies a turning of the head; other prepositions can be used depending on the context
    • auf/nach etwas schauen — to look at something
  6. Austria, Bavaria, Southern-Germany, intransitive, weak to look after, to watch, to take care, to keep an eye on
    • Kannst du bitte auf das Kind schauen? — Could you please keep an eye on the child?
  7. informal, intransitive, weak to decide spontaneously and/or by personal preference; to wait and see
    • Ach, schauen wir einmal, wie sich die Sache entwickelt. — Well, let's wait and see how things develop.

Etymology: From Middle High German schouwen, from Old High German scouwōn, from Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (“to look, see, watch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to heed, look, feel, take note of”). Cognate with Old English scēawian (“to look at, examine, show”). Compare English show.

column5:
noun
  1. feminine sheath, scabbard
  2. feminine vagina
  3. feminine, in-compounds partition, border, limit

Etymology: From Middle High German scheide, from Old High German sceida, from Proto-West Germanic *skaiþiju. Compare Low German scheed, Dutch schede, English sheath, Danish skede, Norwegian Bokmål skjede, Icelandic skeið. The anatomical sense (16th c.) is a calque of Latin vagīna. The sense “partition” is attested since Old High German, but as it is not found in other Germanic languages, it is sometimes considered a later deverbal derivation from the related verb scheiden.

column7:
noun
  1. masculine, strong shine, gleam, flash

    Synonyms: Lichtschein, Schimmer

  2. masculine, strong semblance, appearance

    Synonyms: Anschein

  3. abbreviation, alt-of, ellipsis, masculine, strong certificate, ticket, bill, note; ellipsis of Geldschein: banknote

    Synonyms: Bescheinigung, Nachweis

  4. masculine, slang, strong certificate, ticket, bill, note; A case which a medical professional liquidates by invoice
    • Woher kommt die Einstellung, mindestens 1.200 Scheine im Quartal haben zu müssen? Einige stellen zwei MFA ein, machen 800 Scheine und sind dann weniger gestresst - auch das ist möglich.

    Synonyms: Bescheinigung, Nachweis

  5. masculine, strong certificate, ticket, bill, note; An individual class’s course credit (because till even the 2010s one would actually get a slip of paper)

    Synonyms: Bescheinigung, Nachweis

Etymology: From Middle High German schīn, Old High German scīn, skīn (“shine, brightness, light, ray”), from Proto-West Germanic *skīn, from Proto-Germanic *skīną. Cognate with Old Norse skína, Old Saxon scīnan, Old English sċīn (“phantom, ghost”), Dutch schijn, English shine, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌴𐌹𐌽𐌰𐌽 (skeinan).

column9:
noun
  1. also, masculine, neuter, strong log, billet, stick (of firewood)
    • Beim Hacken des Brennholzes flogen die Scheite fast bis zum Dach. — During the chopping of firewood, the logs went flying and almost hit the roof.

Etymology: From Middle High German schīt, from Old High German scīt (“log of wood”), from Proto-West Germanic *skīd (“piece of wood”). Cognate with West Frisian skīd, Old Norse skíð (“plank; billet; ski”), Old English sċīd, English shide, Ancient Greek σχίζα (skhíza, “splinter”), Latvian skaida (“chip”), Lithuanian skëdrà. Doublet of Ski.

column10:
noun
  1. masculine, strong footstool

    Synonyms: Fußbank

  2. masculine, strong low, simple stool, taboret

    Synonyms: Hocker, Stockerl

Etymology: From Middle High German schemel, schamel, from Old High German scamal, from Proto-West Germanic *skamul, *skamil (“stool, bench”). Doublet of Stabelle.

column5:
noun
  1. feminine pub

    Synonyms: Bar, Beisel, Beisl, Beiz, Bierhalle, Bierhaus, Buvette, Kabacke, Kabache, Kaschemme, Kneipe, Kretscham, Krug, Lokal, Pinte, Pub, Schenke, Schwemme, Spelunke, Stampe, Tschocherl, Trinkhalle, Wirtschaft, Wirtshaus

Etymology: From the verb schenken (“to pour”).

column4:
noun
  1. masculine, strong each of the two main parts of a leg; shank (lower part) or thigh (upper part)
  2. masculine, strong each of the two straight lines that meet in an angle
  3. masculine, strong each of the two sides of equal length of an isosceles triangle

Etymology: From Middle High German schenkel, schinkel, akin to Old High German scanca. More at shank.

column6:
noun
  1. feminine shard, sherd, fragment

    Synonyms: Scherben

Etymology: From Middle High German scherbe, from Old High German scirbi, from Proto-Germanic *skarbōjan-, related to *skrapōną (“to scratch”).

column4:
noun
  1. feminine a pair of scissors, shears
    • Kann ich mir eben deine Schere ausleihen? — Can I borrow your scissors for a minute?
  2. feminine a pair of pincers (on a crab)
  3. feminine, figuratively a gap, especially a widening one
    • die Schere zwischen Arm und Reich — the (widening) gap between the poor and rich

Etymology: From Middle High German schære, from Old High German scāri, plural of scār, from Proto-West Germanic *skeran. The spelling with -e- (instead of Schäre) is East Central German, probably reinforced by the related verb scheren (“to shear”). Cognate with Dutch schaar, English shears.

noun
  1. feminine barn

    Synonyms: Scheuer, Stadel

Etymology: From Middle High German schiune, from Old High German scugin(n)a, from a Proto-Germanic *sku(w)enjō-, for which see Proto-Germanic *skūrō (“shelter, shack”) for more. The word was originally chiefly East Central German versus otherwise predominant Scheuer (Austro-Bavarian also Stadel). Scheune is reinforced by cognate Low German Schüün.

noun
  1. feminine layer, stratum, seam
  2. feminine sheet, ply, coat (e.g. of paint)
  3. feminine class, stratum, group of people with a certain social status
  4. feminine shift (day's work period, the group of people who work a certain shift)
    • Kommste vonne Schicht / Wat schönret gibt et nich' / Als wie Currywurst
  5. feminine stint

Etymology: From northern Middle High German schiht, from Middle Low German schicht, schichte, derived from the verb schichten (whence German schichten). Cognate with Dutch schicht, English shift.

noun
  1. feminine a staff on which something moves; rail
    • Entfernen Sie dieses Fahrzeug von der Schiene. — Remove this vehicle from the rail.
    • Mit dem Geld wollen sie Schienen, Brücken und Bahnhöfe reparieren. — They want to use the money to repair tracks, bridges and train stations.
  2. feminine a staff on which something moves; rack
  3. feminine a staff or long construction that holds things together; orthotics; splint
  4. feminine a staff or long construction that holds things together; frame; skid
  5. feminine busbar

Etymology: Inherited from Middle High German schine, from Old High German skina, from Proto-West Germanic *skinu. Cognate with Dutch scheen, English shin.

column7:
noun
  1. neuter, strong reed
  2. neuter, strong reeds

Etymology: From Middle High German schilf, from Old High German sciluf, from Proto-West Germanic *skilp, *skilup (“reed, rush”).

column4:
noun
  1. feminine shingle
  2. feminine a paddle used in the game of hornussen

Etymology: From Middle High German schindel, from Old High German scintula, from Proto-West Germanic *skindulā (“roof-shingle”).

column8:
noun
  1. masculine, strong screen (movable protective cover); umbrella (thin fabric cover stretched on a frame with a longer shaft)
  2. masculine, strong screen (movable protective cover); bill, peak (of a cap)
  3. abbreviation, alt-of, clipping, masculine, strong clipping of Bildschirm (“screen, monitor”)

Etymology: From Middle High German schirm, scherm, from Old High German skerm, skirm (“screen”), from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi (“fur, pelt, covering, screen”). More at screen. Compare scrim.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine battle
  2. feminine sort, breed

    Synonyms: Art, Gattung, Rasse, Stamm

  3. feminine groyne, breakwater

    Synonyms: Buhne, Buhnenwerk

Etymology: From Middle High German slaht, from Old High German slahta, ultimately from the root of schlagen (“to strike, hit”). Compare Danish slag (“battle, strike”). Cognate of English slaughter.

noun
  1. feminine slag, dross, scoria
  2. feminine cinders, clinker
  3. feminine sediment, dregs, scum
  4. feminine metabolic residue in body tissue or digestive system
  5. dialectal, feminine rectum

Etymology: From Middle Low German slagge (“slag”, older “splinter of hammered iron”, 14th c.), from slān (“to hit, strike”), the cognate of German schlagen. Compare Dutch slak, English slag, both also from Middle Low German.

name
  1. derogatory, humorous, neuter, often, proper-noun, strong FC Schalke 04 (football club of Gelsenkirchen, Ruhrgebiet)

Etymology: Alteration of Schalke based on etymology 1 above, suggested by the club’s origins in, and continued association with, coal mining.

column73:
adj
  1. slack, limp
    • Sie werfen einen Blick in ein Autowrack. Glassplitter liegen im Fußraum, und der schlaffe Airbag ist blutverschmiert. — They take ganders into the crack wreck. Glass shards are lying inside the footwell, and the slack airbag is bloodstained.
  2. weak, weary

Etymology: From Middle High German slaf, from Old High German slaf, from Proto-Germanic *slap-, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂b- (“to be weak, limp, languid”), see also Latin labō (“fluctuate, waver”).     • Sie ist schwanger von ihrem Mann Peter mit ihrem dritten Kind. — She is pregnant from her husband Peter with her third child.

    Synonyms: in anderen Umständen, in Hoffnung, guter Hoffnung

  2. colloquial, not-comparable pregnant, gravid (of animals)

    Synonyms: trächtig

  3. not-comparable, poetic full of, laden with

Etymology: From Middle High German swanger, from Old High German swangar, from Proto-West Germanic *swangr (“heavy”), further origin unknown. Cognate with Old English swangor, Dutch zwanger (“pregnant”), Yiddish שוואַנגער (shvanger, “pregnant”), and Norwegian Bokmål svanger (“pregnant”); compare also Lithuanian sunkùs (“heavy; difficult”).

column9:
noun
  1. masculine, strong swarm of insects; flock of birds; school of fish
    • Dazu zirpten unzählige Zikaden, schillernde Libellen schossen surrend durch die Luft, […], Mücken summten in Schwärmen, […] — In addition countless cicadas chirped, iridescent dragonflies shot buzzingly through the air, […], mosquitoes hummed in swarms, […]
  2. masculine, strong crush; beloved; object of one’s (unfulfilled) love

Etymology: From Middle High German swarm, from Old High German swarm, from Proto-Germanic *swarmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum”). Compare Dutch zwerm, English swarm, Danish sværm. The sense “crush” is a backformation from the verb schwärmen; see there.

column4:
noun
  1. masculine, no-plural, strong swindle

    Synonyms: Betrug

  2. masculine, no-plural, strong dizziness, vertigo

Etymology: From Middle High German [Term?]. Cognate with Hunsrik Schwinnel.

column9:
noun
  1. masculine, strong a swinging motion, sweep
    • Mit einem Schwung warf er alle Akten vom Tisch. — In one sweep he threw all the files off the desk.
  2. masculine, strong a quantity so swept, (hence colloquial) any large amount
    • Sie knallte mir einen Schwung Akten auf den Tisch. — She banged a pile of files onto my desk.
  3. masculine, strong momentum, speed, force (intensity of a specific movement)
    • Du musst mit mehr Schwung über die Rampe fahren, wenn du weiter springen willst. — You need to go over the ramp with more speed if you want to jump further.
    • Er soll die flaue Wirtschaft wieder in Schwung bringen. — His job is to stir the sagging economy.
  4. masculine, strong pep, vim, verve, dash, panache
    • Die Show wirkt altbacken, sie braucht wieder mehr Schwung. — The show feels stodgy, it needs to get some pep back.

Etymology: From Middle High German swunc, ablaut derivation from swingen, modern schwingen (“to swing”). Originally infrequent, but in general use since the 18th century.

column92:
verb
  1. class-3, intransitive, strong to swing (to move back and forth)
    • Sie schwingt auf einer Schaukel. — She is swinging on a swing.
  2. class-3, intransitive, strong to move (somewhere) by swinging
  3. class-3, reflexive, strong, transitive to swing (to move something using a swinging motion)
  4. class-3, strong, transitive to wave; to brandish
  5. class-3, intransitive, strong to vibrate
  6. class-3, intransitive, strong to oscillate
    • Das grundlegende Problem aller optischen Mikroskope ist das Licht: Es schwingt, je nach Farbe, mit einer Wellenlänge von einigen hundert Nanometern. — The fundamental problem of all optical microscopes is the light: it oscillates, depending on the color, with a wavelength of a few hundred nanometers.
  7. class-3, formal, intransitive, strong to resound
  8. class-3, formal, intransitive, strong to propagate (somewhere) as sound, to move throughout (an area) resounding
    • der Klang der Glocken schwang durch die Stadt — the sound of the bells resounded throughout the city
  9. class-3, intransitive, strong to be expressed (in someone's words)
  10. class-3, strong to ski back and forth
  11. class-3, formal, reflexive, strong to arc
  12. class-3, regional, strong to clean (hemp or flax) of wood residues
  13. Switzerland, class-3, strong to wrestle in the Schwingen (Swiss wrestling) style

Etymology: From Middle High German swingen, from Old High German swingan, from Proto-Germanic *swinganą. Cognate with Low German swingen, English swing. Doublet of swingen.

column8:
noun
  1. masculine, strong oath

    Synonyms: Gelübde, Eid

Etymology: From Middle High German swuor, from Old High German swuor, from Proto-Germanic *swōraz (“oath”), from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną (“to speak, swear”). Compare English swear and Vilamovian śwür.

column3:
noun
  1. archaic, feminine, humorous, no-plural, poetic romantic love

    Synonyms: Liebe

  2. Middle-Ages, feminine, historical, no-plural courtly love; a kind of chivalrous, serving love by a knight for a noblewoman, generally secret and sometimes adulterous

Etymology: Borrowed in the Romantic era from Middle High German minne, from Old High German minna (“loving remembrance”); from Proto-West Germanic *minnju, from Proto-Germanic *minjō.

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong blessing
    • im Nachhinein ein Segen — a blessing in disguise
    • Und der weise Greis, mein Meister, gab mir seinen Segen, daß ich Euch aus jenem wunderbaren, mit Unzialschrift geschriebenen Buche einige Gleichnisse, Geschichten und Sagen erzähle. — And the wise old man, my master, gave me his blessing to tell you some parables, stories, and sagas from that wonderful book written in uncial script.

Etymology: From Middle High German segen, from Old High German segan, from Latin signum. Cognate to Low German Siägen (Münsterländisch, Lippisch). Compare English sign.

noun
  1. masculine, strong, uncountable Riesling grape (a variety of grape grown especially in Germany and other relatively cool areas)
  2. masculine, strong Riesling (a white wine made from Riesling grapes)

    Synonyms: Johannisberger, Klingelberger, Moselriesling, Rheinriesling

Etymology: Uncertain. Possibly from a Middle High German variant of rueszling, perhaps ruoz (“soot”), from Old High German hruoz, from Proto-Germanic *hrōtaz (“soot”) + the suffix -ling. The semantic connection with soot would be referring to the grapes' tendency to develop black spots when ripe. There are several written references to the variety of grape dating from the 15th century.

column4:
noun
  1. feminine, usually side (a bounding straight edge of a two-dimensional shape)
    • Ein Dreieck hat drei Seiten. — A triangle has three sides.

    Synonyms: Kante, Flanke

  2. feminine face, side, surface of any three-dimensional object
    • Ein Würfel hat sechs identische Seiten. — A cube has six identical sides.
  3. feminine page (single leaf of any manuscript or book)

    Synonyms: Buchseite, S.

  4. feminine side (one of the two surfaces of a sheet of paper)
    • Du kannst auf beide Seiten des Blattes schreiben. — You can write on both sides of the paper.
  5. feminine one side or half of something or someone
    • Auf der rechten Seite findest du nützliche Info. Die andere Seite ist nutzlos. — On the right side you will find useful information. The other side is useless.
    • Beide Seiten sind unleserlich. — Both sides are illegible.

    Synonyms: Hälfte, Teil

  6. feminine, figuratively a certain aspect of a concept
    • Versuch es einmal von der schönen Seite zu betrachten. — Try to look at it from the bright side.
    • Um ein Problem zu lösen muss man den Sachverhalt von allen Seiten betrachten. — To solve a problem, one has to take into account all the specific aspects of the issue.

    Synonyms: Aspekt, Perspektive, Blickwinkel

  7. feminine, figuratively side, faction or group of competitors in a war, game, conflict or any other competitive situation in opposite to their opponents
    • Keine Seite kann diesen Krieg gewinnen. — No faction is able to win this war.
    • Ich bin immer auf der Seite der Verlierer. — I am always on the side of the losers.

    Synonyms: Fraktion, Team

  8. feminine face of a coin or die
  9. feminine website

    Synonyms: Webseite

Etymology: From Middle High German sît(e), from Old High German sīta, from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ. Cognate with Dutch zijde, Low German Siede, English side, Swedish sida.

column6:

noun
  1. masculine, strong victory

    • Selbst da, wo schon die Revolution unter der Losung „Alle Macht den Räten!“ den Sieg der Arbeiter und Bauern brachte, wurden die Räte staats- und parteiuntertan[…] — Even there, where the revolution, under the slogan "All power to the councils!", already brought the victory of the workers and peasants, the councils became servant to state and party […]

Etymology: From Middle High German sige, sic, from Old High German sigu, sigi, from Proto-West Germanic *sigi, from Proto-Germanic *segaz, from Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- (“related to overpowering”).

column3:
name
  1. feminine, proper-noun Sieg (a river in North Rhine-Westphalia and Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany; a tributary of the Rhine)
    • Die Republikaner wurden über die Sieg zurückgeworfen, und Lefèvbre hatte alle Noth zu entkommen. Schon am 11. November waren die Plünderer bis über die Sieg zurückgelaufen, und die Husaren von Barko und das Regiment Grünlaudon mit den bewaffneten Bauern überschritten noch am nämlichen Tage diesen Fluß. Prinz Würtemberg wählte am 12. November sein Hauptquartier zu Ueckerath, während Lefèvbre bei Troisdorf an der Acher ein Lager bezog und die Nachbardörfer zum Schanzarbeiten und Holzfällen zwang, womit er sich in die Erde vergrub. General Hatry zog gleichzeitig sich durch’s Rheinthal zurück, eine Menge Raubes fortschleppend, der den Lefèvbre’schen wieder abgejagt war. Die Hauptmacht der Franzosen zog mit den geraubten Vorräthen über die Wupper zurück, während Lefèvbre bei Troisdorf sich immer tiefer verschanzte. Leider durfte Prinz Ferdinand den Sieg nicht weiter verfolgen, weil der Hofkriegsrath zu Wien ihm verboten hatte, die Sieg zu überschreiten.

Etymology: From Old High German Sigin (whence Medieval Latin Sigina), either from: * Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- (“related to overpowering”), so called after the force of the water, one gush overtaking the other, then cognate to the Schüß / Schüss / Suze f in Bern, Sionge f in Fribourg, Seyon m in Neuchâtel, Saône f in Eastern France, Sée f in the Normandy; most via Celtic *sego- (“force”); or from * Proto-Indo-European *seykʷ- (“related to filtering”) via Proto-Germanic *sīganą (“to sink”), so called for sinking smoothly out of her mountain, having her vehemence filtered by her path, then cognate to the Simoa in Buskerud, Norway, Seenbach m in Hesse, Siggern f in Solothurn.

column15:

Cognate with Scots sok (“sock, stocking”), West Frisian sok (“sock”), Dutch sok (“sock”), English sock, Danish sok, sokke (“sock”), Swedish sock, socka (“sock”), Icelandic sokkur (“sock”).

column9:
noun
  1. masculine, strong bucket
    • Vom 5. Mai ab konnte nun eine geregelte Vertheilung von Wasser an den Brunnen eintreten. Die Jedem zugetheilte Quantität betrug auf je 3 Mann einen kleinen Spann (Wedro) für 24 Stunden. Die Pferde sollten je einen Spann Wasser für 24 Stunden erhalten, man fand es jedoch praktischer und ökonomischer, Pontons bei den Brunnen zu placiren, diese zu füllen und die Pferde daraus zu tränken. — From the 5th of May on regular distribution of water at the wells could commence. The quantity allotted to everyone was a small bucket (ведро (vedro)) upon three men for 24 hours. The horses were supposed to get a bucket of water each for 24 hours, but it was perceived more feasible and economical to place pontoons at the wells, fill them and drench the horses therefrom.

    Synonyms: Eimer, Kübel

Etymology: Borrowed from Middle Low German span, from Old Swedish spander, Swedish spann.

column4:
noun
  1. masculine, strong spade
  2. colloquial, derogatory, masculine, strong idiot, dumbass

Etymology: The word was originally restricted to Low and Central German: from Middle High German spade, spate and Middle Low German spade, both from Old Saxon spado (possibly also Old High German *spato), from Proto-Germanic *spadô. Due to its northern origin the form has undergone open-syllable lengthening before -t- (which was generally blocked in Upper German). Cognate to English spade; see there for further cognates.

column6:
noun

  2. masculine, mixed, weak house sparrow (Passer domesticus)

column7:

column9:

  3. feminine pungency

noun

    • Die kleine Stutzuhr auf dem Kamin, ein letzter Rest der Habe meiner Eltern, schlug zehn. — The small bracket clock on the chimney, a last remnant of the belongings of my parents, chimed ten.

Etymology: From Middle High German habe, from Old High German haba, from Proto-West Germanic *habu.

column73:
adj
  1. bald, hairless
  2. figuratively barren, bleak, empty, stark, bland

Etymology: From Middle High German kal (inflected kalwe), from Old High German kalo, chalo, from Proto-West Germanic *kalu, from Proto-Germanic *kalwaz (“naked, bald”), from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“naked, bald”). The form kahl (instead of *kalb) is based on the Middle High German uninflected stem. However, the lengthened vowel points to influence by varieties that reduce -lw- to -l- even in open syllables; these include Middle Low German kāl (inflected kāle). See the same development in fahl. Cognate with Dutch kaal, English callow, and further Italian calvo, Russian голый (golyj, “nude”), Persian کل (kal), Romanian chel.

adj
  1. sober (not drunk; serious, not playful or passionate)
  2. on an empty stomach
    • Bitte kommen Sie nüchtern zur Untersuchung. — Please do not eat anything before the examination.
  3. matter-of-fact, unemotional

Etymology: From Middle High German nüehtern, from Old High German nuohtarn, nuohturn, from Latin nocturnus (“nocturnal”). The word was probably originally used among monks in monasteries, with sense development "nocturnal" > "of dawn (the edge of night and day)" > "not having consumed any sustenance yet" > "sober". Compare Danish nøgtern, Hunsrik nichter, English nocturnal.

column5:
noun
  1. feminine rung, rundle, step (of a ladder)
    • Die Leiter hat sechs Sprossen. — The ladder has six rungs.
  2. feminine branch, tine, prong (of an antler)
  3. feminine sprout (outgrowth on a seed or fruit); for a shoot of an actual growing plant, the doublet Spross m is more usual
    • Wenn Kartoffeln länger gelagert werden, bilden sich oft Sprossen. — When potatoes are stored for longer periods of time, they often form sprouts.
    • Warum liegt hier eine Sojasprosse auf dem Boden? — Why is there a soybean sprout lying on the ground?
  4. Austria, abbreviation, alt-of, feminine short for Kohlsprosse (“Brussels sprout”)
  5. abbreviation, alt-of, feminine short for Sommersprosse (“freckle”)
    • Wenn ich bei gutem Wetter draußen bin, kriege ich sofort Sprossen im Gesicht. — Whenever I go outside in good weather, I immediately get freckles on my face.

Etymology: From Middle High German sprozze m, from Old High German sprozzo (“rung”), from Proto-Germanic *sprutô, from the root of *spreutaną, whence sprießen. Cognate with Dutch sport (“rung”), Middle Low German sprōte (“rung, sprout”), Old English sprot(a) (“sprout”). The sense “sprout” seems to be original, but is not attested in High German before the 15th century. Doublet of Spross, which compare. The sense “freckle” (17th c., at first also in the form sprusse) is a semantic loan from Middle Low German sprûte (literally “sprout”), an ablaut variant of the above noun. Cognate with Dutch spruit (“sprout”) and sproet (“freckle”), English sprout.

column53:
verb

    • In seiner Wut fegte der Mann das Geschirr vom Tisch. — In his rage, the man swept the dishes off the table.

column3:

column4:

column97:
adj
  1. stupid, dim-witted

    Synonyms: einfältig, dumm, doof, geistesschwach

    • Dass wir den letzten Zug verpasst haben, ist natürlich blöd. — Us missing the last train is unfortunate, of course.

    • Ich finde einfach den blöden Schlüssel nicht! — I just can't find this stupid key!

Cognate with Old English blēaþ (“gentle, shy, cowardly, timid; slothful, inactive, effeminate”), English blate (“bashful, stupid”) and bloat (“be swollen, be worthless”) and Danish blød (“soft”).

column7:
adj
  1. little, few (a small amount, a small number)

Etymology: From Middle High German weinec, wēnec (“marginal”), from Old High German *weinag, wēnag (“miserable”), from Proto-Germanic *wainagaz. The form with -ei- is original; that with -ē- arose through conflation with the morphologically simpler Old High German wē (“woe”), akin to English woe. The diphthong -ei- later on regularly became -ē- in several dialects, which further strengthened the monophthongal form wenig. Cognate with Dutch weinig, Low German weinig, Hunsrik wenich, Yiddish ווייניק (veynik). The comparative minder comes from Middle High German minder, minre, minner; the Middle High German superlative is minnest, minst. Both are related to min.

column97:
adj
  1. glad; (momentarily) happy; (momentarily) cheerful
    • Ich bin froh über alles, was ich erreicht habe. — I am happy about everything I've achieved.
    • Du wirst deines Lebens nicht mehr froh. — You will no longer be happy with your life.

    Synonyms: fröhlich, glücklich

  2. merry

    Synonyms: fröhlich

  3. merry; hearty; energetic

    Synonyms: beherzt, fröhlich, wacker

Etymology: From Middle High German vrō, from Old High German frō, frao, from Proto-Germanic *frawaz (“quick, glad”). Compare Dutch vrolijk, whence also English frolic.

column3:
name

Etymology: From English Orlando, from Italian Orlando.

column73:
adj
  1. thick, tight, dense
    • Baschir trägt einen dichten Bart, der einzig die Partie zwischen der Oberlippe und seiner großen Nase ausspart. — Baschir wears a dense beard, which only leaves out the part between the upper lip and his big nose.
  2. impermeable, sealed, shut, locked (preventing passage or entrance)
  3. impermeable, sealed, shut, locked (preventing passage or entrance); closed, out of operation, out of business
    • Spätestens 2028 muss etwas kommen – sonst ist der Laden dicht. — In 2028 at the latest, they have to release something - otherwise this place is out of business.
    • dicht machen — to close up, to shutter
  4. close
  5. colloquial tight, intoxicated

    Synonyms: betrunken

Etymology: From Middle High German dīchte, from Old High German dīhti, from Proto-West Germanic *þį̄ht(ī), from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz. The modern vocalism is from Middle Low German dicht(e) with Low German shortening before -cht (compare German leicht and German Low German licht). The expected form deicht is attested in early modern German. Cognate with Dutch dicht, English tight.

column5:
adv
  1. modal, particle just, simply, indicating that something is generally known or cannot be changed, and is therefore to be accepted; often equivalent to a shrug
    • Er ist eben ein Idiot... — He's an idiot, that's just how he is...
    • Dann müssen wir eben härter arbeiten. — Then we'll just have to work harder.

    Synonyms: halt

  2. modal, particle just, quickly, indicating that something is done fast or without much complication
    • Ich geh mal eben zur Theke. — I'll just go to the bar.
    • Könnten Sie mir vielleicht eben helfen? — Could you maybe help me out really quickly?

    Synonyms: kurz

  3. just; a moment ago
    • Wo ist denn dein Mann? Der saß doch eben noch hier. — Where's your husband? He was sitting here just a minute ago.
  4. rare even
    • Und du kannst mir sagen, wie gut (oder schlecht eben...) es ist. — And you can tell me how good (or even how bad...) it is.
  5. literary exactly, very
    • Es sollte eben diese Entscheidung sein, die ihn in den Bankrott treiben würde. — It would be this very decision that drove him into bankruptcy.

    Synonyms: genau

Etymology: The adjective is from Middle High German ëben, from Old High German ëban, the adverb from ëbano; from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz and its adverb equivalent. Cognate with Low German even, Dutch even, effen, English even, Danish jævn.

column6:

column61:
