  2. neuter, proper-noun 11580 Bautzen (an asteroid)

Etymology: From Middle High German Būdessen (and spelling variants), from Old Sorbian. Cognate with Upper Sorbian Budyšin, Polish Budziszyn. First attested in a Medieval Latin text as Budusin in 1002. The German form is an entirely regular outcome of the Slavic: Postalveolar -š- was borrowed as retracted Middle High German -s-, and Modern German diphthongisation and syncope then yielded Bautzen. The further origin is uncertain, but probably Slavic, with suggestions including: * Named after a prince called Budissentius, Budestaus, or alternatively a female *Budiša, from Proto-Slavic *buditi (“to awaken”). Compare names like Budigost, Budimir, Budislav. * Some sources derive it from the Slavic name of the Ortenburg castle in Bautzen, which is given as Budetzsch, but they do not explain it further. A derivation from Upper Sorbian buda (“hut”) is highly unlikely as this is a Germanic loanword. * Bautzen legend/folk etymology explains the name by a tale in which a traveling duchess gave birth in present-day Bautzen, during which the rushing husband asked budeli ssen, or perhaps in modern Upper Sorbian budźe syn? (“will it be a son?”). Compare also Bautzen at German Wikipedia.

Etymology: * (letter) From Alemannic Middle High German aͤ, a representation of secondary umlaut [æ]. In Early Modern German, the letter spread to Central German, which did not have a special phoneme for secondary umlaut. Therefore, ä was seen there as a marker of umlaut as such, and was used analogously. * (sound) Middle High German distinguished up to five stressed e-vowels: [æ], [ɛ], [ɛː], [e], [eː]. Through open-syllable lengthening, mergers, and analogy, this system was not just reduced but entirely altered. 19th-century Standard German generally retained only one short vowel, but distinguished [ɛː] from [eː]. All long ⟨ä⟩s were by then usually pronounced [ɛː], while ⟨e⟩ was [ɛː] in some words, [eː] in others. The choice between these, however, varied greatly from region to region, and was entirely absent in many Low German areas. Theodor Siebs therefore (consistently but rather arbitrarily) restricted [ɛː] to the spelling ⟨ä⟩ in his codification of stage and broadcasting German. Unintendedly, this reinforced the tendency towards total merger as the dialectal systems of distinction were disturbed.

For front soldiers, Bahnhof (“train station”) would have been synonymous with furlough or relocation to the hinterland, so the phrase would originally have meant “to understand only what one wants to hear”, “not to pay attention”. What may corroborate this theory is the variant immer Bahnhof verstehen (literally “to understand train station all the time”). Other suggested origins: * Train stations are noisy, hectic places with whirring engines, shouting passengers, unintelligible announcements etc. * The word Bahnhof (and its equivalents in other languages) would typically have been familiar to international travellers even if they knew hardly any other word of the local language.

In favour of Pfeifer is the fact that the first concentration camp, Dachau, was in Upper German territory and many early inmates came from the workers' movement and trade unions, who could have introduced the dialectal term Kapo (“site foreman”) (construction slang). Compare also East Franconian Kapo, Rhine Franconian Kapo, Alemannic German Capo, all meaning "foreman". Although plausible, the folk-etymology which assumes a direct loan from Italian capo (“boss, chief”) suggested by occasional spellings Capo, Lagercapo and no-doubt reinforced in later times by the Italian term's dissemination in the wake of the Godfather trilogy has not been substantiated. Etymology: 20th century, from Low German and Central Franconian dialects. Cognate to Dutch friemelen (“to fiddle, fidget”). Probably the same as Dutch and Middle Dutch wriemelen (“to move back and forth”, intransitive and transitive), Low German wrimen (“to rub”), with a development from wr- to fr-, which is widespread among dialects of all the relevant languages. Philippa (Etymologisch Woordenboek, 2003-09) casts doubt on this because wriemelen also means “to swarm” (of a collective). This collective sense need not be the oldest, however. In fact, the first attestation has the sense “to move back and forth with exertion” (of a man during sexual intercourse), and the sense “to fiddle, fidget” is attested for the wr-form as well. Philippa prefers to derive friemelen from frommelen (“to fidget”) and this in turn from fommelen (German fummeln). However, frommelen shows variants with wr- as well and is also regionally more restricted.

Etymology: Literally, “my name is Hase”, but often reinterpreted as “My name is hare”. because the underlying anecdote is not generally known. In 1854, Heidelberg student Victor von Hase gave his ID card to a fellow student, so the latter could flee to France; when the ID was later found, Hase was questioned by the university, and he replied: Mein Name ist Hase, ich verneine die Generalfragen, ich weiß von nichts. Etymology: Early 20th century, originally Berlin slang. By surface analysis, pusten (“to blow”) + Kuchen (“cake, pie”). The word Kuchen on its own is already attested with the same sense in thieves' cant (Rotwelsch) since 1818, and likely goes back to Yiddish חכם (khokhem, “wise or cunning man”), used here with a sense along the lines of “you wise guy!” or “you trickster!”. The first component may be Yiddish פּשוט (poshet, “simply”), but this appears less conclusive. It may also be merely the verb pusten in the sense “to exhale/snort dismissively”; compare the expression jemandem etwas pusten/husten (“to refuse outright”).

Etymology: From Middle High German lest, a contraction of leȥȥest, from Old High German leȥȥist (also laȥȥōst), itself superlative of laȥ (cognate to English late). The modern German form with -tz- is of northern origin; two separate origins have probably met in it: Firstly, there is a general tendency in some Central German dialects of inserting -t- before comparative and superlative endings. (Compare for this, for example, Ripuarian fröh → fröhter, fröhtste). Secondly, Middle Low German lest, contracted superlative of lat (“late”), had a regular or regularized variant letst, which is very rare in writing, but may have been more common in spoken dialects. (Compare modern German Low German lättst.) Related forms are Dutch laatst and lest, English latest and last, Luxembourgish lescht, Hunsrik letst.

Etymology: From Middle High German hanthaben (1349). The earliest sense is “to keep, protect, maintain”, hence eventually a loan translation of Old French maintenir and/or Latin manūtenēre. The possible French origin and the earlier attestation of Middle Dutch hanthaven (1286) and Middle Low German handhafen (1330) suggest that the word may have been borrowed through these. The Germanic formation must be denominal, which is particularly obvious in the northern languages (where the verb “to have” is hebben), but is also seen in High German from the invariably regular conjugation. The nominal element may be Middle High German hanthabe (“haft, handle”), from Old High German hanthaba, anthaba (also Old Saxon handhava; Middle Dutch hanthave only attested 1490), but the semantics seem problematic. Alternatively a new compound from hant + Middle High German habe, Middle Dutch have (“possession, belongings”); cf. Middle High German hanthab (“stolen good”, ca. 1350).

The traditional association with Romansh davo(s) (“behind”) is a folk etymology and is incompatible with the historical forms, which regularly begin with T-. Schorta later proposed an alternative derivation from Latin *octāvātum (“eighth”), perhaps referring to an economic or administrative division, but this is less likely.

    • Hier finden sich dann die Dasselbeulen, etwa sechs Monate nach dem Schwärmen der Fliegen, also im Januar bis zum Frühjahr. Die Beulen erreichen die Größe einer Walnuß und weisen bei der Reife seitlich eine kleine Öffnung auf, aus der eine klebrige Flüssigkeit hervortritt. In diesen Beulen sitzen die Larven, von den Landleuten „Engerlinge“ genannt. — Here the warbles appear, approximately six months after the swarming of the adult, thus in January until the Spring. The swellings reach the size of a walnut and upon maturity exhibit a small opening at the side, from which a sticky fluid emerges. In these swellings reside the larvae, known to the country folk as "grubs".

  1. neuter, no-plural, strong cupronickel

Etymology: From Kupfer (“copper”) + Nickel (“mischievous spirit or demon”). This word originated as a pejorative German term for ores of the element nickel, whose bright green color closely resembles malachite, an otherwise reliable indicator of valuable copper ore. However, like iron, nickel ore is impossible to smelt at the relatively low temperatures needed to smelt copper. (This is also why the Copper Age preceded the Iron Age.) Annoyed at wasting their time on such ore, German miners began calling it cupfernickel, that is, "copper demon." When chemists eventually identified and named the element in the ore, they shortened the name of the ore to nickel. The name of this element thus has the same roots as the phrase "Old Nick," which refers to a supreme devil or demon. Feeling a bit whimsical, chemists of that same period named another newly isolated iron-like element, cobalt, after a mischievous German household spirit, the "kobold".

column56:
verb
  1. informal, intransitive, weak to cheat (especially in games, but also in business, school, etc.)

    Synonyms: mogeln, schwindeln

Etymology: There are two main theories, which need not be mutually exclusive but may complement each other. * From dialectal schummeln, originally probably “to move back and forth”, whence various attested senses: “waver, totter; rock, swing, push; chase off; abscond, steal away; take clandestinely; rummage; bustle about; do housework”, etc. In favour of this derivation speaks that the sense “to cheat” was sometimes associated with “trickery through swift movements”, especially in the context of gambling. The verb schummeln (in the above-mentioned senses) is found in dialects as far south as Tyrol, but Adelung considered it chiefly Low German and the earliest attestations are of late Middle Dutch scommelen (1410: “to do kitchenwork”, 1530: “to rock, move back and forth”); hence probably of northern origin through Middle Low German *schummelen, eventually perhaps onomatopoeic. Compare modern Dutch schommelen. Compare also German verschaukeln (“to cheat”), from schaukeln (“to rock, swing”). * Through a dialectally attested sense “to trade (of a Jewish merchant)”, from Yiddish שום (shum), an acronym for the cities of Speyer, Worms, Mainz, the so-called Schum cities, old centres of Jewish religion and trade. However, a verb derived from this acronym is not attested in Yiddish and the sense “to trade” may be derived from the sense “to cheat”, rather than vice versa.

    • Und schon geht Günter wieder zur Tagesordnung über – schließlich läuft die Firma jetzt. Alles ist Friede, Freude, Eierkuchen. Der Erfolg kommt scheinbar wie von selbst, schön regelmäßig und jedes Jahr zur gleichen Saison. — And Günter is already settling into the daily routine—after all, the company is up and running now. Everything’s A-okay. Success seems to be coming on its own, at regular intervals and at the same time every year.

  2. colloquial knock on wood; a superstitious expression used to avoid the negative consequences of some utterance
    • Bisher hat alles gut geklappt – toi, toi, toi. — So far it has all worked out well – touch wood!

Etymology: Attested since the 19th century. Spread more generally through various songs of the 1920s and 1930s. Widely considered onomatopoeic for spitting. Spitting out three times is a superstitious act that remains common in several European as well as non-European cultures. In polite circles this was considered rude and hence replaced with the onomatopoeia. Compare Swedish tvi, imitative of spitting and used as a spoken onomatopoeia alternative to spitting three times to ward off bad luck. Compare also the idea of touching wood, the equivalent of which in German-speaking Europe is to knock on wood three times. It is possible, though unprovable, that the specific form of the onomatopoeia might have been reinforced by the word Teufel (“devil”, with the superstitious idea that saying something negative will have a positive effect, compare Hals- und Beinbruch) or by Yiddish טוב (tov, “good”).

  3. neuter, proper-noun a farming community in eDumbe local municipality, Zululand district municipality, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa

Etymology: From Middle Low German Lü̂neborch, from an Old Saxon name attested in Latinised form as Luniburc (mid-10th century). The Old Saxon is generally construed as *Hliuniburg, after an identified placename Hliuni that occurs in the annals of Charlemagne (ca. 800). This in turn is usually considered a derivative of hlēo (“hill, burial mound, dam, bastion, shelter”), from Proto-Germanic *hlaiwą. Compare the Westphalian placename Lünen. On the other hand, it seems clear that the similarity to the Polabian name of the town Glain, Glein, Chlein can hardly be coincidental. The Polabian might be from Germanic, but it has also been connected with Proto-Slavic *glina (“clay, loam”).

Etymology: An onomatopoeic word liable to alteration and variation. Formally iterative of obsolete hechen, heichen (“to pant”), a chiefly Central and Low German word; compare Middle Low German hīgen, heigen, hēgen (“to pant”), from or related with Proto-West Germanic *hīgōn (whence Dutch hijgen, English hie). Another obsolete variant German hechzen is derived from or reinterpreted as the interjection hach! + the old suffix -zen (“to say something”). Further compare hauchen. Middle High German hecheln, hacheln is attested in the sense “to copulate”, which might be derived from underlying “to pant”, though this is rather unlikely. The sense exists also in the above-mentioned Middle Low German hīgen and in this language it is probably due to influence by hīwen (“to marry, to copulate”, later “to rape”; see Dutch huwen, Luxembourgish geheien, German Heirat). In Middle Low German and Middle Dutch, this feminine noun would have widely merged with the aforementioned wāch, wāg per open-syllable lengthening.

East, German, especially, masculine, regional, strong A stone (to be found at the coasts of the Baltic Sea) with generally one, but at times several, naturally formed holes (usually used as amulet, talisman or mascot) being in most cases a flint nodule whose chalk deposits are washed out or weathered; self-bored stone, ≈ adder stone
    • Ein Hühnergott – das ist ein Meeressteinchen mit einem kleinen Loch. Man sagt, die Krimtataren hätten geglaubt, daß ein solches Steinchen, mit einem Faden an die Hühnerstange gehängt, das Federvieh zu verbesserter Legetätigkeit ansporne. Daher auch der Name Hühnergott. Später kam der Glaube hinzu, ein Hühnergott bringe auch den Menschen Glück. Mir scheint, ein bißchen glaubt jeder an solche Glücksbringer: die einen mit kindlich-vertrauensseliger Offenheit, die anderen heimlich, mit mürrischer Verbissenheit. Ich glaube heimlich daran. Immer wenn ich am Meer war, wünschte ich mir sehr, einen Hühnergott zu finden, aber in diesem Sommer ganz besonders. — A self-bored stone – that is a small stone found by the sea with a little hole [in it]. It is said of the Crimean Tatars that they had believed such a small stone, hung up on a hen roost by a thread, would spur the poultry on to improved laying activity. Thus the [self-bored stone′s local] name “hen′s god”. Later the belief additionally arose that self-bored stones would bring people good luck. It appears to me that everyone believes in such lucky charms: some with childlike-credulous openness, others privily, with grumpy doggedness. I privily believe in it. Every time I had been by the sea I wished so hard to find a self-bored stone, but especially in this summer.
    • Während die einen am Strand nach Bernstein, Hühnergöttern oder Donnerkeilen suchen, ernten andere Schilf, um damit Dächer zu decken. — While some search on the beach for amber, self-bored stones or thunderbolts, others harvest reed to thatch roofs with it.

Etymology: * Huhn (“chicken, hen”) + Gott (“god”) with epenthesis of -er including umlaut. * The origin of the word is unclear. Theories For a time it was suspected that the word was introduced into German via the loan translation made by Thomas Reschke in 1966 of an expression already occurring in the original title of the Russian novella called “Куриный бог” written in 1963 by Yevgeny Yevtushenko. Owing to the novella the stone and its name gained, from 1966 onwards, great popularity in the former GDR. In 1985 it was introduced in the 18th revision of the East German version of “Der Große Duden” dictionary of German orthography. Widely unknown in Western Germany, the word appeared for the first time in 1999 in the 3rd edition of the – now all-German – ten-volume dictionary “Duden, Das große Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache”; one year later it found its way into the 22nd edition of the dictionary of German orthography, “Duden, Die deutsche Rechtschreibung”. However, the word seems to already have existed in German before 1966.: in the year of publication of the Soviet original version in 1963, it already occurs in a first translation made by René Drommert published in the West German daily “Die Zeit”. A decade before, it is attested in the first volume of the German translation – made by Alexander Böltz and published by the publishers Rütten & Loening – of the Russian novel “Iwan Ⅲ.” by Valery Yasvitsky. The oldest known attestation up to now occurs, however, in a book by Dmitry Tselenin about the Russian (East-Slavic) folklore published in German in 1927 by de Gruyter publisher′s in which the Russian expression “Kuriny bog” [written in Latin letters] is translated into German as “Hühnergott”. And yet, there is even now, however, no solid proof and no reliable evidence for the usage of the word “Hühnergott” in German before 1966. From a folkloristic point of view it is interesting that the word first only existed in the GDR, but not to the west of the Elbe river, which is without a doubt attributable to the distribution of Yevtushenko′s novella in the translation by Reschke. Even though the German word existed – for instance in reference books or through private contacts – sporadically here and there, Thomas Reschke′s credit for introducing the word “Hühnergott” into the German language usage and its ultimate canonization in the “Duden” dictionaries remains therefore irrefutable.

Etymology: From Kadaver + Gehorsam, lit. "cadaverous obedience", "corpse-obedience" or "corpse-like obedience" (Porter 2013). Ultimately a rendition of an expression in the Constitutiones by Ignatius of Loyola (1558), qui sub Obedientia vivunt, se ferri ac regi a divina Providentia per Superiores suos sinere debent perinde, ac si cadaver essent . This expression was satirized by critics of the Jesuit order in Germany after 1814, in the German translation wie wenn sie ein Cadaver wären. The equivalent French expression as coined by Eugène Sue (1845) was obéissance de cadavre or obéissance cadavérique. The German compound appears in the 1870s, in the context of the 1872 prohibition of the Jesuit order in Germany. The German term also entered usage as a loanword in other European languages, and by the 20th century it was applied more typically to the blind loyalty in Prussian militarism rather than in the Jesuit order.

Etymology: From Old High German brūtlouft, reanalyzed as Braut (“bride”) + Lauf (“run, walk”). This reanalysis is etymologically correct since Old High German -louft is derived from loufan (modern laufen). The formation is of Proto-Germanic origin: compare Old Saxon brūdloht, Middle Dutch bruloft (whence modern Dutch bruiloft), and slightly differing Old English brȳdhlop, Old Norse brúðhlaup (whence Swedish bröllop, Danish and Norwegian bryllup). The semantics behind this compound are uncertain. Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną probably meant “to leap, jump”, which would point to the wedding celebration (compare Dutch huwelijk). However, the sense “to run” may also be old, in which case a reference to the taking-home or ritualized abduction of the bride becomes very suggestive. The latter idea is preferred in much of the literature.

  1. masculine, strong A headdress, head finery, especially of women, or regal finery like a crown.
    • [Seine Frau], ich versichere Dich, sieht heute so aus, wie sie gestern aussah und morgen aussehen wird. Der Kopfputz wie vor zehn Jahren und länger, immer glatt, fest, bescheiden. — His wife, I assure you, looks today like she looked yesterday and will look tomorrow. The head finery is like ten years before and longer, always straight, tight, humble!
    • Auch die Bekleidung der Männer hat nichts Ausgezeichnetes, aber um so eigenthümlicher ist, wie es von allen Reisenden hervorgehoben wird, die der Weiber! Denn auf dem Kopfe tragen sie eine hohe Mütze von Birkenrinde in Gestalt eines abgestumpften Kegels, welche mit blauem Tuche überzogen und auf der vordern Seite dicht mit Silbermünzen besetzt ist. Über die selbe wird ein großes weißes, an den Ecken mit Figuren ausgenähtes und mit rothen Frangen eingefaßtes Tuch gehängt, so daß der kurze Zipfel vorn über die Mütze, der lange aber über den Rücken hinabhängt, während die Seitentheile auf den Schultern ruhen. Unter diesem Kopfputz wird das Haar zusammengerollt und versteckt, denn sie schämen sich dasselbe sehen zu lassen und legen sich daher, wenn Fremde in dem Hause übernachten, mit diesem Kopfputz sogar schlafen, so wie sie damit auch die Arbeit in den Viehställen verrichten; dieser Kopfputz heißt bei ihnen Aischon. — Also, the apparel of the men has nothing notable, but the more peculiar is, as all travellers stress, the one of the women! For on the head they wear a high cap of birch bark in the shape of a truncated cone, which is overlaid by blue cloth and on the front side stuffed with silver coins. Over the self-same they hang a large white blanket sewn out on the corners with figures and framed with fringes, so that the short cusp hangs ahead down the cap, but the long one down the back, while the side parts rest on the shoulders. Under this head finery the hair is rolled together and hidden, for they shun letting it see and lay themselves, when foreigners spend the night in the house, with this head finery to bed, as they also do their work in the animal stable with it; this head finery is called Aischon with them.

  1. masculine, strong flange (projecting edge at the end of component (esp. of metal) to fasten to or anchor with other parts, now especially of pipes)
    • Die Zunge b besteht aus einem starken vierkantigen Eisen, und ist von demselben oben nur so viel abgehobelt, als der Radflansch erfordert. — Switch b consists of a strong, square piece of iron, and from its top exactly enough has been abraded as is required by the flange of the wheel.
    • Mittels Schrauben und Muttern werden beide Flansche mit der Dichtung verbunden. — Both flanges are tightened to the seal using nuts and bolts.

Etymology: According to Kluge, Pfeifer and Duden, from Middle High German vlansch (“corner, end”), with possible relations to Flunsch (“pout, pouty mouth”) and to flennen (“to cry noisily, snivel”). However, the likely descendant of the inherited term seems to show very little usage in New High German, and with the sense having shifted towartds "torn bit, strip of meat". The modern meaning of "flange" appears fairly suddenly in the first half of the 19th century specifically in engineering. This sense, or any close to it, is markedly absent in Grimm's dictionary despite being contemperaneous. The closeness in sense and form could alternatively suggest a borrowing from English flange, flanch.

column56: <p-n>verb</p-n> <ol><li><p-tags>weak</p-tags> to grumble (make a low sound, as of a discontent person, an empty stomach, a distant thunderstorm)<ul><li><i>Für die geringe Beteiligung macht Reitz vor allem die Unzufriedenheit innerhalb der Partei verantwortlich – eine Unzufriedenheit, die er als strukturell beschreibt:

column1: „Die SPD ist ja 'ne Grummelpartei.“ Die Genossen seien keine „Partei der Optimisten“, sondern Menschen, „die strukturell unzufrieden sind“. Die Sozialdemokraten seien „die Nöl- und Nörgelpartei“, deren Daseinszweck darin liege, das Leben verbessern zu wollen – was ihr jedoch „niemals gelingt“. Entsprechend sei die aktuelle Beteiligung von gut 50 Prozent sogar „vergleichsweise viel“. — For the low turnout Reitz makes responsible discontent within the party, in particular—a discontent he describes as structural:

”The SPD, to wit, is a grumble party.” It would not be a “party of optimists” but people who are “structurally disconcerted”. The social democrats would be “the party of bickering and bellyaching”, whose sole purpose of existence is to improve wellbeing in life—in which they “never succeed”. To accord with this, the present turnout of about 50 percent is “relative high”.

Etymology: From Low and Central German dialects, from Middle Low German grummelen and northern Middle High German *grummeln, iterative of grummen. A relation with Gram and grimmig is theoretically possible, but the words certainly have a strong onomatopoeic element. Cognate with Dutch grommelen, English grumble.

    • Bedenken begegnet in erster Linie die Ansicht des Berufungsgerichts, es fehle an einer Übergabe der Steine, weil die von der Firma Schl. und der Beklagten einverständlich getroffenen Maßnahmen keine ausreichende räumliche Herrschaftsbeziehung der Beklagten zu den Steinen hergestellt hätten. Entscheidend für die Besitzfrage ist, worauf auch das Berufungsgericht abhebt, die Verkehrsauffassung. Unter diesem Gesichtspunkt kann es, entgegen der Ansicht des Berufungsgerichts, nicht darauf ankommen, daß der zur Bewachung abgeordnete Angestellte der Beklagten nicht Tag und Nacht »auf« den Steinen saß. Auch an zur Nachtzeit nicht bewachten Sachen besteht nach der Auffassung des Verkehrs der an Tage offen in die Erscheinung tretende Besitz weiter. Ferner ist die Annahme des Berufungsgerichts bedenklich, ein unmittelbarer Besitz der Beklagten sei hier nicht möglich gewesen, weil die Steine nach wie vor auf dem eingezäunten Werksgelände der Firma Schl. lagerten und diese deshalb, den Abtransport jederzeit verhindern und die Steine selbst wegschaffen konnte. Dabei wird nicht hinreichend berücksichtigt, daß damit die Firma Schl. gegen ihre vertraglichen Pflichten verstoßen hätte; ein Wille dazu kann nicht ohne weiteres unterstellt werden und wird auch nicht schon durch den vom Berufungsgericht erörterten Einzelfall nahegelegt. Ferner waren die bei einem Abtransport tätig werdenden Arbeitnehmer der Firma Schl. - vom Verkaufsleiter bis zum Nachtwächter - darüber informiert, daß die Steine der Beklagten gehörten und deshalb nur mit deren Einverständnis abgefahren worden durften. Es hätte also besonderer gegenteiliger Anordnungen seitens der Firma Schl. bedurft, um wieder die tatsächliche Verfügungsgewalt über die Steine auszuüben, wobei der von der Beklagten abgeordnete Wächter offen oder durch heimliches Vorgehen bei Nacht oder während einer sonstigen Abwesenheit des Wächters hätte ausgeschaltet werden müssen. Es braucht aber letztlich nicht entschieden zu werden, ob bei einem solchen Sachverhalt die Verkehrsauffassung trotz der fortbestehenden theoretischen Zugriffsmöglichkeit des Verkäufers nicht unmittelbaren Alleinbesitz des Käufers bejaht und deshalb hier die Voraussetzungen einer Übereignung mittels Übergabe nach § 929 BGB gegeben waren. Selbst wenn man das verneint, so sind hier die Steine in jedem Fall, wie die Revision zutreffend geltend macht, gemäß § 930 BGB mittels Vereinbarung eines Besitzkonstituts an die Beklagte übereignet worden.

Semantic derivation disputed. The Duden dictionary suspects a learned jocular translation from Latin olet mihi (“I smell [something]”) (with dative construction as in German), due to phonetic similarity of Latin olēre (“to smell”) and olor (“swan”). Grimm however, because of the early and near-contemporaneous attestations in different regions, sees it as an inherited word of the common people, connecting it to the traditional Germanic association of swans with prophecy and fate (cf. the Norns) and pointing to the synonymous expression Schwansfedern haben/tragen (literally “to have/wear swan's feathers”). Earlier variants contain -d- (schwanden, Low German swanden), probably under influence of ahnden, a once common variant of ahnen (“to anticipate, to suspect”).

Diese schon durch das stete Bücken äusserst beschwerliche Arbeit wird immer, wie bei uns das Graben, zugleich von mehreren verrichtet, und daher kommt das in die Spanische Sprache übergegangene Sprichwort: son de una misma laya, sie sind eines Gelichters. — The great difficulty which soil cultivation has to surmount in Biscaya, is the hardness and strength of the bottom. They till it therefore not only multiple times in succession, but also employ some peculiar instruments. The most peculiar under them is the laya. It consists in a long and spiky two-pronged fork with a short shaft, which however isn’t fastened in the middle, but at one end. Each labourer has two such forks in his hand, sticks them horizontally into the earth, pushes them, with one, or peradventure with both feet simultaneously treading on them, even deeper, and tears then, pushing the shaft down to him, a whole bit of lawn at once aloose and turns it over. This job onerous already by way of the constanting stooping is always, as with us graving, performed at the same time by many, and hence comes the saying passed into Spanish: son de una misma laya, they are of one kind.

Etymology: From Middle High German gelihter (“siblings, kin”), from Old High German lëhtar, gilëhtar (“womb, matrix”), a derivative of ligan, modern liegen (“to lie, to recline”). Since the seventeenth century often despective.

Etymology: From Middle High German krieche, from Old High German *kriehha (attested in kriehboum). Cognate with Middle Dutch crieke (modern kriek), Middle Low German krêke (modern Kreke, Kreike). Further origin uncertain, but predominantly believed to be from Proto-West Germanic *Krēkō (“Greek”). The fruit in question may have been spread along the Danube, but “Greek” might also have been used simply in the sense of “foreign, novel”. The challenge to this etymology lies in the fact that no reference to a “Greek” fruit is found in Medieval Latin (prunum graecum appears only in the 16th c. in Germany). An alternative theory therefore reconstructs West Germanic *kreuku (“crooked or misshapen tree/fruit”), which would be akin to *krukkju (“crutch”). Further cognates All borrowed from continental West Germanic languages: Danish kræge, Norwegian kræge, Swedish krikon, English crocket, Old French creke, creque (French crèque), Old Prussian krichaytos (with some suffix), Lithuanian kryklė, Latvian kriķis

Etymology: From Low German Pinöpel, from Middle Low German pinappel, pināpel, pinākel (“roundish ornament at the top of a steeple”), itself borrowed from Latin pinnāculum.     • Stille Waſſer waren oft tief. Mancher hatte es fauſtdick hinter den Ohren. — Stil waters were known to run deep. Some people were slyer than foxes.

    • Es fing so harmlos an, das Extrakonzert am Mittwochabend. Doch das Glöckchenklingen und Vögelchenzwitschern wuchs sich aus und hatte es am Ende faustdick hinter den Ohren. — It all started so innocently at the special concert on Wednesday evening. But the ringing of the bells and the chirping of birds was mushrooming and eventually turned into something unexpectedly powerful.

    Synonyms: es in sich haben, nicht ohne sein

Etymology: Literally, “to have it fist-thick behind the ears”. The idiom is rooted in the old popular belief that waggishness and trickiness were little demons that sat behind people’s ears and were recognizable by thick bumps or lumps. Compare the German idiomatic expressions den Schalk im Nacken haben, jemandem sitzt der Schalk im Nacken, jemandem sitzt der Schalk hinter den Ohren.

The sense “snotnose”, which Pfeifer considers original, is of very limited attestation and not mentioned at all by early sources such as the Low German dictionaries of Dähnert (1780) and Schütze (1806). Nevertheless it is plausible to associate the onset S(ch)n- with words like Schnabel (“beak”, cf. Grünschnabel), Schnute (“snout”), Schnodder (“snot”, cf. schnodderig). The latter portion of the word seems to be derived from, or at least influenced by, Low German unnösel (cognate of Dutch onnozel). This adjective has a variety of negative meanings ranging from “naive, silly” to “brazen, ill-mannered”, all of which fit the sense “presumptuous young man” well. Cognate with Dutch sneuzel (“greenhorn”), which is a recent acquisition from eastern dialects, however.

The Germanic name for the river is attested as Rusa or Rusia from the 9th century, and was occasionally recorded as Ursa in the Early Modern period (compare Urseren). This name likely derives from the early Germanic *Rūsi or the oblique form *Rūsjō-. Greule (1982) interprets the name as an Old European hydronym, closely related to Riß. Given Ptolemy’s record of the pre-Germanic name Silana, it is possible that only part of the river was known as Rūsi in antiquity. Alternatively, Rūsi may have been introduced as a Germanic name during the early medieval period, potentially derived from Old High German rūsa, riusa (“fish trap”) (see the modern Reuse). column1: Trotz jenen Entscheidungen ist natürlich noch lange nicht daran zu denken, daß dem Unfug einer als gänzlich falsch erkannten Aussprache des Griechischen ein Ende gesetzt wäre. Der Schlendrian wird auf diesem Gebiete des Schulwesens wohl ebenso lange dauern, wie auf vielen andern; denn bequem ist allerdings jener Schlendrian, nur wissenschaftlich ist er nicht, und unbrauchbar für das Leben ist er obendrein. Die Beseitigung des Schlendrians werde ich wohl nicht mehr erleben, auch dann nicht, wenn Plato selber aus der Asche auferstünde und die deutschen Schulmänner die richtige Aussprache lehrte. Sie würden ihm beweisen, daß er sich irre: er habe in den mehr als zwei Jahrtausenden seit seinem Tode gewiß die richtige Aussprache vergessen; sie aber, die deutschen Oberlehrer und Direktoren, kennten sie ganz genau: sie wäre buchstäblich so wie das Neuhochdeutsche des 20. Jahrhunderts gewesen. — So these are the reckonings of the greatest scholars about the not quite insignificant question how one of the languages which is taught to about 50 000 young lads per annum should be pronounced.

In spite of these reckonings by far it is not to think that this buffoonery of an utterly wrong pronunciation of Greek would come to an end. The litherness in this field of schooling will last as long as in many others; for convenient it is forsooth, but scientific it is not, and devoid of use for life ’tis on top. The elimination of this litherness I will not be an observer of in my lifetime, even if Plato himself were to rise from his ashes and teach the pedants the right pronunciation. They would shew him his being at fault: he surely has forgot the right pronunciation; but them, the senior and head teachers know it very well; it would be literally like the New High German of the 20th century.

The form Neune suggests origin in East Central German, where such nominalized numerals in -e are common, perhaps specifically Berlin. Etymology: From Westphalian Low German wulla(c)ken (attested 19th c. or earlier), also walla(c)ken and, without the velar element, wullen. All of these have the sense “to beat, brawl” besides “to toil”. Perhaps most plausibly a corruption of buerwiärken, from Middle Low German bûrwerken (“to perform obligatory services in public construction, groundworks etc.”), derived from bûr (“citizen, burgher, villager, farmer”) + werken (“to work”). Compare the byform bollwiärken (“to toil”), which was influenced by the noun at hand in English bulwark. The Westfälisches Wörterbuch also attests a form bullackern, which may reflect an intermediate step of the further development. Other possible connections These include: * Low German wöhlen, German wühlen (“to dig, rummage”); * Low German Wull, German Wolle (“wool”), either through the noun Wullaken (“firm fabric of wool and flax”), or as in sich in die Wolle kriegen (“to brawl, fight”); * Low German Wallack, German Wallach (“gelding”, hence “working horse”); * (Low) German walken (“to waulk, full, beat”); * (Low) German ackern (“to toil”), from Acker (“field, agricultural land”). Note that even if the derivation from buer-, bollwiärken is correct, some of these influences may explain the phonetic form, especially the initial w-.

Etymology: First attested as Oipen in 1213. From Middle Dutch Oepen, Oipen, Oupen, Open. According to the prevalent theory from Proto-West Germanic *opan (“open”). The Middle Dutch spellings indeed seem to point to a back vowel; on the other hand there is no certainty about this and the modern front-rounded vowel would remain unexplained. An alternative theory derives it from *up (“up, at the top”) + *-īn. This explains the umlaut, but is still at odds with the dialectal pronunciation [ˈøˑʏ̯pə] ~ [ˈøːpə], which would require West-Germanic au-. Therefore a third theory postulates an underlying *Aupīn, in which *aup- would be a blend of *auwju (“floodplain”) with the hydronym *apa-. The spelling in Eu- appears in the 16th century and is probably a Franco-Flemish representation of [øː]. The contemporary Standard German pronunciation may to some degree be a spelling pronunciation, but it also approaches the local [øˑʏ̯], which moreover generally corresponds to standard eu, äu.

Immediately comparable with Dutch tod, English tod (“bush, flock”), and perhaps Old Norse toddi (“piece”). Also related with Old High German zata, zato (“flock”), Old Norse taða (“manured meadow”), from Proto-Germanic *tadǭ. Probably from the root Proto-Indo-European *deh₂- (“to split, cut, divide”).   1. feminine surplus store (store selling a variety of excess, expired, obsolete or otherwise unwanted goods)

    • „Ab kommender Woche wird es bei uns zugehen wie an einer Resterampe“, sagt Klambt. — "Starting next week, it's going to be like a surplus store at our shops," Klambt says.
  2. definite, feminine, figuratively, usually leftovers, bottom of the barrel (figurative location for ideas, things or people without notable positive qualities, to be used when nothing better is available)
    • Merchandising betreibt [Harald] Schmidt auch und Zurückhaltung sehe ich in Kalendern mit ollen Sprüchen oder Büchern mit noch älteren Kolumnentexten nicht. […] Merchandising sehe ich nicht als verwerflich an - wenn es gut gemacht ist. Und da ist mir ein eigenständiger und neuer Artikel wie das Computerspiel oder die Songs von Raab (von der Substanz ganz abgesehen) immer noch lieber als Harrys Resterampe. — [Harald] Schmidt also does merchandising, and I don't see any restraint in his calendars with lame platitudes or books with even older editorials. […] By itself I don't see merchandising as objectionable - if it's done well. And in that regard, I'd still rather take a standalone and new item like the video game or Raab's songs (actual content aside) over Harry's Bargain Bin.
    • So wirkt Streamin' With wie die Resterampe der Aufnahmetermine, routiniert mit kleinen Höhepunkten gespielt und willkürlich zusammengestellt. — As it stands, Streamin' With comes across as the cutting-room leftovers of the recording sessions, played well-practiced with small highlights and then arbitarily compiled.

Etymology: Based on the surplus goods chain "Rudis Reste Rampe" (lit. "Rudi's Ramp of Leftovers"), references to which occur starting in the late 1980's in Berlin. The choice of the term Rampe (“ramp”) is likely at least partly motivated by the alliteration, but potentially from the sense of "(un)loading dock", see Laderampe. Early metaphorical applications in the 1990's and early 2000's often still reference the full name of the store, using it for wordplay with other people named Rudi, or substituting other names. By the 2010's, it had become significantly more common to simply refer to "(die) Resterampe".

These then came to be distinguished in such a way that the short-vowel form expressed stationary location (adverb of in + dative), while the long-vowel form expressed movement (adverb of in + accusative). This distinction is largely maintained in modern German (cf. darin vs. hinein). Accordingly the prefix inne- is generally used with stationary verbs.

column2:
proverb
  1. You should treat others as you want to be treated by them.

Etymology: Literally, “don’t do to others what you don’t want done to yourself”. The phrase is a calque of Latin quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris, which has been ascribed to Severus Alexander. Possibly based on the golden rule (Matthew 7:12), but at least associated with it later on. Compare Dutch wat gij niet wilt dat u geschiedt, doe dat ook een ander niet. The spelling of dass or das in the second clause varies in practice, but the correct form is the conjunction. Compare an alternative phrase with a preposition, such as wovon du nicht willst, dass man spricht, which shows that it cannot be an accusative pronoun. The form tu is third-person singular present subjunctive (short for tue).

  2. dated, derogatory, sometimes pietistic, filled with deep religiosity, possibly rapturous or zealous

Etymology: From Gott (“God”) + selig (“blissful, blessed”, older also “gracious, pious”). Coined by Luther in the 16th century. He intended it to express the simple, natural piety of a true believer who performs good works only to honour God (neither hoping for reward nor fearing punishment).     • Kürzlich schockierte mich die Sprache eines sogenannten XXL-Ostfriesen im norddeutschen N3-Fernsehen. Er sagte: „Dann habe ich halt dem Peerd das Achterbeen wieder eingerenkt… das kann ich nun mal halt ganz gut!“ Was hat mich an dieser […] Rede […] so empört, beziehungsweise tieftraurig gestimmt? So what about this speech made me so upset, or rather deeply disappointed? Well, it's that twice-used, trendy filler word “halt…”. Since about ten or twenty years ago, that “halt” can be heard everywhere – whether you're halt in line at the supermarket or halt asking someone for directions or halt relaxing at the beach on Wangerooge.
    • Diese beiden Tipps helfen Ihnen, kürzere Sätze zu formulieren und damit ganz automatisch Pausen einzubauen: […] Sie gehen sparsamer mit „und-Konstruktionen“ um.   • Der Begriff „Talahon“ beschreibt eine Gruppe von Jugendlichen mit bestimmten Eigenschaften. Man meint damit meist junge Männer im Alter zwischen 10 und 25 Jahren, die in der Öffentlichkeit rumhängen. In der Regel bezieht sich „Talahon“ auf Männer mit einem migrantischen Hintergrund. Dabei weisen sie einige stereotypische Merkmale auf. Dazu gehören „Männer-Handtaschen“ und (meist gefälschte) Bauchtaschen von Marken wie Gucci, EA7-Jacken, Fußball-Trikots von internationalen Teams wie Paris St. Germain oder AC Mailand, Nike-Schuhe, Cappys, nach außen hängende Goldketten und Jeans oder Jogging-Hosen sowie Airpods, die in den Ohren hängen, auch wenn man sich untereinander unterhält. Eine gegelte Mittelscheitelfrisur, Einweg-Vapes und Energy-Drinks vor allem von Red Bull gehören ebenfalls zum Erscheinungsbild der Talahons. — The term "Talahon" describes a group of young people with certain characteristics. It usually refers to young men between the ages of 10 and 25 who hang out in public. "Talahon" usually refers to men with a migrant background. They have some stereotypical characteristics. These include "men's handbags" and (mostly fake) fanny packs from brands such as Gucci, EA7 jackets, football jerseys from international teams such as Paris St. Germain or AC Milan, Nike shoes, caps, gold chains hanging outwards and jeans or jogging pants, as well as AirPods that hang in their ears even when talking to each other. A gelled middle-parted hairstyle, disposable vapes and energy drinks, especially from Red Bull, are also part of the Talahons' appearance.

    • Etymology: From South Levantine Arabic تعال لهون (taʕāl la-hōn, “come here”); cf. Maltese talahawn. The expression became popularized in August 2022 by the Syrian rapper Hassan Tammo, with the track “Ta3la hon” (see quote). Its use was amplified over time through Internet culture; by the summer of 2024 it had become general Gen Z slang.

    • Für alle Deutschen, denen die Existenz des Deutschen Reichs eine Selbstverständlichkeit geworden war, die sich bis in den Volksmund niederschlug (»Solang’ das Deutsche Reich besteht, wird jede Schraube rechts gedreht«), bedeutet die Entwicklung auf nationaler Ebene seit dem »Zusammenbruch« von 1945 eine schmerzhafte Identitätskrise, noch weiter kompliziert durch den Kalten Krieg und das Ende der europäischen Kolonialherrschaft nach dem Zweiten Weltkrieg. — For all Germans, for whom the existence of the German Reich had become a matter of course, something that was reflected in popular sayings (“As long as the German Reich exists, every screw will be turned to the right”), the developments at the national level since the “collapse” of 1945 have meant a painful identity crisis, further complicated by the Cold War and the end of European colonial rule after the Second World War.
    • Packte ihn, schleppte ihn zuerst in die Werkstatt: »Solang das Deutsche Reich besteht, wird jede Schraube rechts gedreht.« — [He] grabbed him and first dragged him into the workshop: “As long as the German Reich exists, every screw will be turned to the right.”

Etymology: Literally, “as long as the German Reich exists, the screw will be turned to the right”. Origin unclear. The convention that (most) screws tighten clockwise likely predates the German Reich (1871–1945). Possibly from the belief that the German Reich would exist forever, so saying "as long as the German Reich exists" would emphasize that the following rule will also hold true forever. Attested since the 1970s (see quotations) but possibly much older, especially if the etymology above is correct.

column4:
phrase
  1. humorous Expresses that the lack of something is a marginal issue, because what is there is still very good.
    • „Ich habe leider nur Crémant und keinen Champagner!“ – „Naja, in der Not schmeckt die Wurst auch ohne Brot!“ — “Unfortunately I only have crémant instead of real champagne!” – “Ah well, if there’s no bread, one must eat sausage without it!”
  2. humorous Said when someone eats some fine food pure without the usual side dish.
  3. rare beggars can't be choosers

Etymology: Literally, “in [times of] need, sausage tastes [good] even without bread”, jocular alteration of in der Not schmeckt jedes Brot.

    • Denglisch vs. Zangendeutsch ¶ Sascha, welches befürwortest du? — Denglish vs. Zangendeutsch ¶ Sascha, which one do you prefer?
    • Das haben die von /r/kreiswichs, welche es wiederum von Krautchan haben. Es nennt sich Zangendeutsch und viele, die es zum ersten Mal entdecken, fühlen dieses unglaubliche Verlangen, es auch überall sonst anzuwenden. — They took it from r/kreiswichs, who got it from Krautchan in turn. It's called Zangendeutsch and many people, once they've discovered it, feel an incredible urge to use it everywhere else as well.

Etymology: Compound of Zange (“(pair of) pliers”) + -n- + Deutsch (“German”), said to have originated or been popularized on Krautchan, a German-language imageboard created in 2007. Due to its lack of archiving, the exact context of its coining is likely undiscoverable. The word is attested by 2011. A possible motivation for the compound is that it involves intentionally atypical word usage and formation in German, metaphorically using tools to bend words into shape—compare mit der Brechzange, a variation of mit der Brechstange (“forced, by brute force”, literally “with the crowbar”). It could also be a play on Angelsächsisch (“Anglo-Saxon”), reinterpreted as Angel (“fishing rod”) + Sächsisch.

Das allseits erwartete Suppenkoma, also das Nachmittagstief, bleibt auf diese Weise aus. — In my seminars, I regularly do these exercises with my participants after lunch. column5:

  1. feminine world reserve currency (a reserve currency of global importance)
    • Der US-Dollar gilt seit Jahrzehnten als die wichtigste Weltreservewährung. — The US dollar has been considered the most important world reserve currency for decades.

column4:
noun

    • Die Energiepreisbremse soll Haushalte vor extrem steigenden Kosten schützen. — The energy price brake is intended to protect households from extremely rising costs.

Etymology: Energie (“energy”) + Preis (“price”) + Bremse (“brake”)

noun
  1. feminine electricity price cap, electricity price brake (a government-mandated subsidy or ceiling on electricity costs)
    • Die Strompreisbremse entlastet Verbraucher bei den monatlichen Abschlägen. — The electricity price brake relieves consumers regarding their monthly installments.

Etymology: Strom (“electricity”) + Preis (“price”) + Bremse (“brake”)

noun
  1. feminine gas price cap, gas price brake (a government-mandated subsidy or ceiling on natural gas costs)
    • Die Bundesregierung führte die Gaspreisbremse ein, um die Industrie zu entlasten. — The federal government introduced the gas price brake to relieve the industry.

Etymology: Gas (“gas”) + Preis (“price”) + Bremse (“brake”)

noun
  1. feminine heat price cap, heating price brake (a government-mandated subsidy or ceiling on district heating costs)
    • Mieter mit Fernwärmeanschluss profitieren von der Wärmepreisbremse. — Tenants with district heating connections benefit from the heating price brake.

Etymology: Wärme (“heat”) + Preis (“price”) + Bremse (“brake”)

column6:
noun

    • Die Veruntreuung von Anlegergeld führte zum sofortigen Zusammenbruch des Fonds. — The embezzlement of investor funds led to the immediate collapse of the fund.

noun
  1. neuter, strong donation money, donated funds (money that has been collected through donations)
    • Die Organisation garantiert, dass das Spendengeld direkt bei den Bedürftigen ankommt. — The organization guarantees that the donation money reaches those in need directly.

Etymology: Spende (“donation”) + Geld (“money”)

column4:
noun
  1. feminine world domination, world dominion (supreme political or military control over the entire earth)
    • In vielen Filmen strebt der Bösewicht nach der Weltherrschaft. — In many films, the villain strives for world domination.
    • Historiker diskutieren oft darüber, ob Napoleon tatsächlich die Weltherrschaft anstrebte. — Historians often debate whether Napoleon was actually striving for world dominion.

Etymology: Welt (“world”) + Herrschaft (“dominion, rule”)

noun
  1. feminine world stature, world standing, global significance (the state of being recognized or influential on a global scale)
    • Die deutsche Automobilindustrie genießt seit Jahrzehnten eine enorme Weltgeltung. — The German automotive industry has enjoyed enormous world stature for decades.
    • Durch diese Entdeckung erlangte der Forscher schlagartig wissenschaftliche Weltgeltung. — Through this discovery, the researcher suddenly attained scientific global significance.

Etymology: Welt (“world”) + Geltung (“validity, worth, standing”)

noun
  1. neuter, strong voting behavior, voting pattern, voting record (the manner in which a person or group casts their vote in a political or formal context)
    • Das Abstimmungsverhalten der Abgeordneten wird oft von der Fraktionsdisziplin bestimmt. — The voting behavior of the representatives is often determined by party discipline.
    • Man analysierte das Abstimmungsverhalten Deutschlands in den Vereinten Nationen. — They analyzed Germany's voting record in the United Nations.

Etymology: Abstimmung (“vote, ballot”) + s + Verhalten (“behavior, conduct”)

column6:
noun
  1. Switzerland, neuter, strong the electorate, the body of voters (the collective of citizens entitled to vote, especially in the context of a referendum or direct democracy)
    • Das Schweizer Stimmvolk lehnte die Initiative mit knapper Mehrheit ab. — The Swiss electorate rejected the initiative by a narrow majority.

column5:

column8:
noun
  1. neuter, strong consumer sentiment, consumer confidence, consumer climate (the degree of optimism that consumers feel about the overall state of the economy and their personal financial situation)
    • Das Konsumklima in Deutschland ist auf den tiefsten Stand seit Jahren gefallen. — Consumer confidence in Germany has fallen to its lowest level in years.

Etymology: Konsum (“consumption”) + Klima (“climate”)

noun
  1. neuter, strong economic climate, economic sentiment, business climate (the overall condition and future outlook of an economy, reflecting the confidence of businesses and consumers)
    • Ein stabiles politisches Umfeld ist entscheidend für ein gesundes Wirtschaftsklima. — A stable political environment is crucial for a healthy economic climate.

Etymology: Wirtschaft (“economy”) + -s- (“genitival interfix”) + Klima (“climate”)

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong location factor, locational factor (a condition or characteristic that influences the choice of a specific site for a business or industry)
    • Die Verfügbarkeit von Fachkräften ist heute der wichtigste Standortfaktor für Technologieunternehmen. — The availability of skilled labor is the most important location factor for technology companies today.

Etymology: Standort (“location”) + Faktor (“factor”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong location competition, locational competition (the rivalry between different regions or countries to attract businesses, investment, and skilled labor by offering favorable conditions)
    • Durch die Senkung der Unternehmenssteuern will das Land seine Position im internationalen Standortwettbewerb stärken. — By lowering corporate taxes, the country aims to strengthen its position in the international location competition.

Etymology: Standort (“location”) + Wettbewerb (“competition”)

column8:
noun
  1. neuter, strong investment climate, investment environment (the economic and political conditions in a country that affect whether individuals and businesses are willing to invest capital)
    • Hohe Energiekosten und bürokratische Hürden belasten derzeit das deutsche Investitionsklima. — High energy costs and bureaucratic hurdles are currently weighing on the German investment climate.

Etymology: Investition (“investment”) + -s- (“genitival interfix”) + Klima (“climate”)

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong systemic competition, competition between systems (the rivalry between different social, political, or economic systems to prove their superiority in terms of efficiency, prosperity, and legitimacy)
    • Der globale Systemwettbewerb zwischen demokratischen und autoritären Modellen prägt die aktuelle Geopolitik. — The global systemic competition between democratic and authoritarian models shapes current geopolitics.

Etymology: System (“system”) + Wettbewerb (“competition”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong competition of ideas, design competition, contest (a competition to find the best creative solution, concept, or plan for a specific problem or project)
    • Die Demokratie lebt vom ständigen Ideenwettbewerb der politischen Parteien. — Democracy thrives on the constant competition of ideas between political parties.
    • Für den Neubau der Bibliothek wurde ein internationaler Ideenwettbewerb ausgeschrieben. — An international design competition was announced for the new library building.

Etymology: Idee (“idea”) + n (“interfix”) + Wettbewerb (“competition”)

column4:

    • Die mittelständischen Unternehmen sind der Motor der deutschen Innovationskraft. — Medium-sized companies are the engine of German innovative strength.

Etymology: Innovation (“innovation”) + -s- (“genitival interfix”) + Kraft (“power, force, strength”)

noun
  1. feminine research and development, R&D (creative and systematic work undertaken to increase the stock of knowledge, including knowledge of humanity, culture, and society, and to devise new applications of available knowledge)
    • Die Ausgaben für Forschung und Entwicklung sind im letzten Jahr deutlich gestiegen. — Spending on research and development increased significantly last year.

    • Er arbeitet seit fünf Jahren in der Abteilung für Forschung und Entwicklung. — He has been working in the Research and Development department for five years.

column8:

noun

Etymology: Bulle (“bull”) + -n- (“genitival interfix”) + Markt (“market”)

noun

    Synonyms: Baisse, Abwärtstrend

Etymology: Bär (“bear”) + -en- (“interfix”) + Markt (“market”)

noun

noun

noun
  1. masculine, strong price gain, capital appreciation, increase in value (the amount by which the price of a security has increased over a specific period)
    • Dank des starken Tech-Booms verzeichnete das Portfolio einen beachtlichen Kurszuwachs. — Thanks to the strong tech boom, the portfolio recorded a remarkable price gain.

    Synonyms: Kursgewinn, Wertzuwachs, Kursanstieg

Etymology: Kurs (“price, course”) + Zuwachs (“growth, increase, gain”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong price decline, fall in share price (a downward movement in the value of a security or index)

    Synonyms: Kursabschwächung, Kursminderung, Abwärtsbewegung

Etymology: Kurs (“price, course”) + Rückgang (“decline, decrease, fall”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong price plunge, crash, nosedive (a sudden and very sharp drop in the value of a security or the entire market)
    • Ein enttäuschender Ausblick auf das nächste Quartal löste bei der Aktie einen Kurssturz von 15 Prozent aus. — A disappointing outlook for the next quarter triggered a 15 percent price plunge in the stock.

noun

noun
  1. masculine, strong price collapse, slump (a sudden, significant, and often structural drop in prices, frequently breaking through previous support levels)

    Synonyms: Kurssturz, Kursrutsch, Baisse

Etymology: Kurs (“price, course”) + Einbruch (“collapse, breaking in, slump”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong downtrend, downward trend (a sustained period of declining prices)
    • Trotz kleinerer Erholungen bleibt die Aktie im langfristigen Abwärtstrend. — Despite minor recoveries, the stock remains in a long-term downtrend.
  2. general, masculine, strong downward trend, decline, deterioration (a general development toward a worse or lower state)
    • Die Umfragewerte der Regierung zeigen einen deutlichen Abwärtstrend. — The government's polling numbers show a clear downward trend.

Etymology: abwärts (“downward”) + Trend (“trend”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong uptrend, upward trend (a sustained period of rising prices)
    • Die Chartanalyse bestätigt einen intakten Aufwärtstrend bei den Technologiewerten. — Chart analysis confirms an intact uptrend in technology stocks.
  2. general, masculine, strong upward trend, uptick, improvement (a general development toward a better, higher, or more successful state)
    • Nach Jahren der Stagnation verzeichnet der Arbeitsmarkt endlich einen Aufwärtstrend. — After years of stagnation, the labor market is finally showing an upward trend.

Etymology: aufwärts (“upward”) + Trend (“trend”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong sideways trend, horizontal trend (a market condition where prices remain within a relatively stable range without a clear upward or downward direction)
    • Nach der Rallye im Frühjahr ist die Aktie in einen monatelangen Seitwärtstrend übergegangen. — After the rally in spring, the stock moved into a months-long sideways trend.
  2. general, masculine, strong stagnation, plateau (a period of little or no change in a development or statistical series)
    • Bei den Verkaufszahlen zeigt sich aktuell ein stabiler Seitwärtstrend. — The sales figures are currently showing a stable sideways trend.

Etymology: seitwärts (“sideways”) + Trend (“trend”)

column5:
noun
  1. masculine, strong structural change, structural transformation (a long-term and fundamental change in the basic structure of an economy or society)
    • Das Ruhrgebiet ist ein klassisches Beispiel für den Strukturwandel von der Kohle- und Stahlindustrie hin zu Dienstleistungen. — The Ruhr area is a classic example of structural change from the coal and steel industry toward services.

    Synonyms: Umstrukturierung, Transformation, Neuordnung

Etymology: Struktur (“structure”) + Wandel (“change, transformation”)

column4:
noun
  1. feminine tertiarization (the process of transition to a service-based economy)
    • Die Tertiärisierung hat in den letzten Jahrzehnten dazu geführt, dass über 70 Prozent der Erwerbstätigen im Dienstleistungssektor arbeiten. — Tertiarization has led to over 70 percent of employees working in the service sector in recent decades.

    Synonyms: Dienstleistungsgesellschaft, Sektorwandel

Etymology: Derived from Latin tertiarius (“concerning the third part”), from tertius (“third”), + suffix -ierung.

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong primary sector (the sector of an economy making direct use of natural resources)
    • Die Forstwirtschaft und der Bergbau sind wesentliche Bestandteile des Primärsektors. — Forestry and mining are essential components of the primary sector.

    Synonyms: Urproduktion, Rohstoffsektor

Etymology: primär (“primary”) + Sektor (“sector”).

column4:
noun
  1. feminine adaptability, transformability, versatility (the ability of a system, organization, or individual to undergo fundamental change to adapt to new environmental conditions)
    • In Zeiten der Digitalisierung ist die Wandlungsfähigkeit eines Unternehmens sein wichtigster Wettbewerbsvorteil. — In times of digitalization, a company's adaptability is its most important competitive advantage.

    Synonyms: Anpassungsfähigkeit, Transformationsfähigkeit, Flexibilität, Agilität

Etymology: Wandlung (“transformation, change”) + -s- (“genitival interfix”) + Fähigkeit (“ability, capability”)

column5:
noun
  1. masculine, strong sectoral change (the shift in the relative importance of different economic sectors within an economy)
    • Der Sektorwandel beschreibt den Übergang von der Agrar- zur Industrie- und schließlich zur Dienstleistungsgesellschaft. — Sectoral change describes the transition from an agrarian to an industrial and finally to a service society.

    Synonyms: Strukturwandel, Drei-Sektoren-Hypothese

Etymology: Sektor (“sector”) + Wandel (“change, transformation”)

column4:
noun
  1. feminine deindustrialization (the reduction of industrial activity or capacity in a region or economy)
    • Kritiker warnen, dass hohe Energiepreise zu einer schleichenden Deindustrialisierung des Standorts Deutschland führen könnten. — Critics warn that high energy prices could lead to a creeping deindustrialization of Germany as a business location.

    Synonyms: Industrieabbau, Entindustrialisierung

Etymology: de- + Industrialisierung.

column26:
adj
  1. not-comparable cross-sectoral, cross-industry, trans-sectoral (affecting or relating to more than one industry or field of business)
    • Die Digitalisierung ist ein branchenübergreifender Megatrend. — Digitalization is a cross-industry megatrend.
    • Wir suchen nach branchenübergreifenden Lösungen für das Entsorgungsproblem. — We are looking for cross-sectoral solutions for the disposal problem.

    Synonyms: sektorübergreifend, interdisziplinär, universell

Etymology: Branche (“branch, industry”) + übergreifend (“overarching, across”).

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong secondary sector (the sector of an economy concerned with the processing of raw materials into finished goods)
    • Durch die Automatisierung sinkt die Zahl der Beschäftigten im Sekundärsektor kontinuierlich. — Due to automation, the number of employees in the secondary sector is continuously decreasing.

    Synonyms: Industriesektor, verarbeitendes Gewerbe

Etymology: sekundär (“secondary”) + Sektor (“sector”).

noun
  1. masculine, strong tertiary sector (the segment of the economy that provides services to consumers and other businesses)
    • In hochentwickelten Volkswirtschaften entfallen über 70 Prozent der Bruttowertschöpfung auf den Tertiärsektor. — In highly developed economies, over 70 percent of gross value added comes from the tertiary sector.

    Synonyms: Dienstleistungssektor, Dienstleistungsbereich

Etymology: tertiär (“tertiary”) + Sektor (“sector”).

noun
  1. masculine, strong quaternary sector (the sector of the economy based on knowledge, information technology, and highly specialized services)
    • Die Ansiedlung von Softwarefirmen und Forschungsinstituten stärkt den Quartärsektor der Region. — The settlement of software companies and research institutes strengthens the region's quaternary sector.

    Synonyms: Informationssektor, Wissenssektor

Etymology: quartär (“quaternary”) + Sektor (“sector”).

column4:
noun
  1. feminine primary production (the extraction of natural resources as the first stage of the economic production process)
    • Die Urproduktion umfasst Wirtschaftszweige wie Landwirtschaft, Forstwirtschaft und Bergbau. — Primary production includes economic sectors such as agriculture, forestry, and mining.

    Synonyms: Primärsektor, Rohstoffgewinnung

Etymology: ur- (“original, proto-”) + Produktion (“production”).

noun
  1. feminine raw material extraction, extraction of resources (the process of obtaining natural resources from the earth or environment)
    • Die Rohstoffgewinnung im Tiefbau ist oft mit hohen Sicherheitsrisiken verbunden. — Raw material extraction in underground mining is often associated with high security risks.

    Synonyms: Extraktion, Abbau, Förderung

Etymology: Rohstoff (“raw material”) + Gewinnung (“extraction, gain”) From Rohstoff + Gewinnung (from the verb gewinnen).

noun
  1. feminine raw material processing (the industrial conversion of extracted natural resources into semi-finished or finished products)
    • Die Rohstoffverarbeitung in der Metallurgie erfordert enorme Mengen an Energie. — Raw material processing in metallurgy requires enormous amounts of energy.

    Synonyms: Veredelung, Weiterverarbeitung, Materialverarbeitung

Etymology: Rohstoff (“raw material”) + Verarbeitung (“processing”).

noun
  1. feminine resource scarcity, scarcity of resources (a situation where the demand for a resource exceeds its available supply)
    • Die zunehmende Ressourcenknappheit bei seltenen Erden verteuert die Produktion von Smartphones. — The increasing resource scarcity of rare earths makes the production of smartphones more expensive.

    Synonyms: Mangel, Verknappung, Engpass

Etymology: Ressource (“resource”) + Knappheit (“scarcity”)

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong raw materials sector, commodity sector (the segment of the economy involved in the discovery and extraction of raw materials)
    • Anleger schichten ihr Kapital vermehrt in den Rohstoffsektor um, um sich gegen Inflation abzusichern. — Investors are increasingly shifting their capital into the commodity sector to hedge against inflation.

    Synonyms: Primärsektor, Extraktionssektor

Etymology: Rohstoff (“raw material”) + Sektor (“sector”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong service sector (the portion of the economy that produces intangible goods)
    • Der Übergang zur Dienstleistungsgesellschaft hat den Dienstleistungssektor massiv aufgebläht. — The transition to a service society has massively expanded the service sector.

    Synonyms: Tertiärsektor, Dienstleistungsgewerbe

Etymology: Dienstleistung (“service”) + Sektor (“sector”)

column5:
noun
  1. mixed, neuter service industry, service trade (businesses and trades that provide services rather than tangible goods)
    • Zum Dienstleistungsgewerbe zählen sowohl die Gastronomie als auch die Unternehmensberatung. — The service industry includes both catering and management consultancy.

    Synonyms: Dienstleistungssektor, Tertiärsektor

Etymology: Dienstleistung (“service”) + Gewerbe (“trade, industry”)

column4:
noun
  1. feminine exploration (the search for and assessment of mineral, energy, or other natural resources)
    • Die Kosten für die Exploration neuer Lithium-Vorkommen sind in den letzten Jahren stark gestiegen. — The costs for the exploration of new lithium deposits have risen sharply in recent years.

    Synonyms: Lagerstättensuche, Erkundung, Prospektion

Etymology: Latin exploratio (“scouting, examination”).

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong information sector (the part of the economy that is knowledge-based and focuses on information services)
    • Durch das Internet hat der Informationssektor den industriellen Sektor als wichtigsten Wirtschaftszweig abgelöst. — Through the internet, the information sector has replaced the industrial sector as the most important branch of the economy.

    Synonyms: Quartärsektor, Wissenssektor

Etymology: Information (“information”) + Sektor (“sector”)

column4:
noun
  1. feminine media industry, media economy (the business sector dedicated to the production and distribution of media content)
    • Die Medienwirtschaft befindet sich durch Streaming-Dienste in einem radikalen Umbruch. — The media industry is undergoing a radical transformation due to streaming services.

    Synonyms: Medienbranche, Kreativwirtschaft

Etymology: Medien (“media”) + Wirtschaft (“economy”)

noun
  1. feminine platform economy (an economic system where digital platforms facilitate interactions and transactions between different parties)
    • In der Plattformökonomie gewinnt oft derjenige, der das größte Netzwerk kontrolliert. — In the platform economy, the one who controls the largest network usually wins.

    Synonyms: Plattform-Kapitalismus, Netzwerkökonomie

Etymology: Plattform (“platform”) + Ökonomie (“economy”)

noun
  1. feminine knowledge society (a society in which the creation, distribution, and manipulation of information and knowledge has become the most significant economic and cultural activity)
    • In einer Wissensgesellschaft ist lebenslanges Lernen eine Grundvoraussetzung für beruflichen Erfolg. — In a knowledge society, lifelong learning is a basic prerequisite for professional success.

    Synonyms: Informationsgesellschaft, postindustrielle Gesellschaft

Etymology: Wissen (“knowledge”) + Gesellschaft (“society”)

noun
  1. feminine industrial society (a society driven by the use of technology to enable mass production, supporting a large population with a high capacity for division of labour)
    • Die klassische Industriegesellschaft war durch rauchende Schornsteine und große Fabrikanlagen geprägt. — The classic industrial society was characterized by smoking chimneys and large factory complexes.

    Synonyms: Industriezeitalter, Moderne

Etymology: Industrie (“industry”) + Gesellschaft (“society”)

noun
  1. feminine information society (a society where the creation, distribution, and manipulation of information is the most significant economic and cultural activity)
    • In der modernen Informationsgesellschaft ist der Zugang zum Breitbandinternet ein Grundbedürfnis. — In the modern information society, access to broadband internet is a basic need.

    Synonyms: Wissensgesellschaft, postindustrielle Gesellschaft, Netzwerkgesellschaft

Etymology: Information (“information”) + -s- (“genitival interfix”) + Gesellschaft (“society”)

noun
  1. feminine digital divide (the gulf between those who have ready access to computers and the internet, and those who do not)
    • In ländlichen Gebieten vertieft die mangelnde Breitbandanbindung die digitale Kluft. — In rural areas, the lack of broadband connectivity deepens the digital divide.

    Synonyms: Digital Divide, digitale Spaltung

Etymology: digitale (“digital”) + Kluft (“chasm, rift”)

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong knowledge sector (the part of the economy based on intellectual activities such as R&D, IT, and education)
    • Investitionen in den Wissenssektor gelten als entscheidend für die langfristige Wettbewerbsfähigkeit eines Landes. — Investments in the knowledge sector are considered crucial for a country's long-term competitiveness.

    Synonyms: Quartärsektor, Informationssektor

Etymology: Wissen (“knowledge”) + -s- (“genitival interfix”) + Sektor (“sector”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong bull market, stock market rally (a period of rising stock prices and investor optimism)
    • Der jüngste Börsenaufschwung wurde vor allem durch die starken Gewinne im Wissenssektor getrieben. — The recent stock market rally was primarily driven by strong profits in the knowledge sector.

    Synonyms: Hausse, Bullenmarkt, Kurshöhenflug

Etymology: Börse + Aufschwung

noun
  1. masculine, strong key interest rate, benchmark interest rate (the rate set by a central bank to influence monetary policy)
    • Um die Inflation zu bekämpfen, hat die Zentralbank den Leitzins erneut angehoben. — To combat inflation, the central bank has raised the key interest rate once again.

    Synonyms: Referenzzinssatz, Zentralbankzins

Etymology: leiten (“to lead”) + Zins (“interest rate”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong reference interest rate, benchmark rate (an interest rate used as a basis for calculating other interest rates or for financial contracts)
    • Der EURIBOR ist der wichtigste Referenzzinssatz für kurzfristige Euro-Kredite. — The EURIBOR is the most important reference interest rate for short-term Euro loans.

    Synonyms: Basiszinssatz, Benchmark-Zins

Etymology: Referenz (“reference”) + Zinssatz (“interest rate”)

noun
  1. neuter, strong main refinancing instrument (the primary monetary policy tool used by the ECB to provide liquidity to the banking system)
    • Über das Hauptrefinanzierungsinstrument steuert die EZB die Geldmenge im Euroraum. — The ECB controls the money supply in the eurozone via the main refinancing instrument.

    Synonyms: Hauptrefinanzierungsgeschäft

Etymology: Haupt + Refinanzierung + Instrument

column4:
noun
  1. feminine liquidity management (the process of monitoring, analyzing, and optimizing a company's or bank's liquid assets)
    • Eine effiziente Liquiditätssteuerung ist für Unternehmen im kapitalintensiven Rohstoffsektor überlebenswichtig. — Efficient liquidity management is vital for survival for companies in the capital-intensive raw materials sector.

    Synonyms: Cashmanagement, Liquiditätsplanung

Etymology: Liquidität (“liquidity”) + -s- (“control/management”) + Steuerung

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong liquidity shortage, cash crunch (a temporary situation where cash outflows exceed cash inflows, hindering the ability to meet short-term obligations)
    • Trotz voller Auftragsbücher geriet das Startup aus dem Wissenssektor in einen gefährlichen Liquiditätsengpass. — Despite a full order book, the startup from the knowledge sector ran into a dangerous liquidity bottleneck.

    Synonyms: Zahlungsschwierigkeiten, Liquiditätsklemme, Finanzierungsloch

Etymology: Liquidität (“liquidity”) + -s- (“bottleneck/shortage”) + Engpass

column4:
noun
  1. feminine solvency, ability to pay (the state of having enough assets and cash flow to meet financial obligations)
    • Die Sicherung der Zahlungsfähigkeit hat im Finanzmanagement oberste Priorität. — Securing solvency is the top priority in financial management.

    Synonyms: Liquidität, Solvenz, Bonität

Etymology: Zahlung (“payment”) + -s- (“genitival interfix”) + fähig (“able”) + -keit (“-ity”)

noun
  1. feminine profit distribution (the payment of a portion of a company's net profit to its shareholders or partners)
    • Die Aktionäre stimmten einer Erhöhung der Gewinnausschüttung auf der Hauptversammlung zu. — The shareholders approved an increase in the profit distribution at the annual general meeting.

    Synonyms: Dividendenzahlung, Entnahme

Etymology: Gewinn (“profit”) + Ausschüttung (“distribution/pouring out”)

noun
  1. feminine plowback, retention of profits (the practice of retaining earnings within a company to fund future growth rather than distributing them as dividends)
    • Durch konsequente Gewinnthesaurierung konnte das Startup seine Forschung im Wissenssektor ohne Bankkredite finanzieren. — Through consistent retention of profits, the startup was able to fund its research in the knowledge sector without bank loans.

    Synonyms: Selbstfinanzierung, Gewinneinbehaltung

Etymology: Gewinn (“profit”) + Thesaurierung (“accumulation/hoarding”) From Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “treasure, storehouse”).

noun
  1. feminine financial clout, purchasing power (the actual capacity of an entity to deploy liquid funds for purchases or investments)
    • Die enorme Zahlungskraft des Investors ermöglichte die Übernahme des Konkurrenten innerhalb weniger Tage. — The investor's enormous financial clout enabled the takeover of the competitor within a few days.

    Synonyms: Finanzkraft, Kaufkraft, Liquidität

Etymology: Zahlung (“payment”) + -s- (“genitival interfix”) + Kraft (“power/force”)

noun
  1. feminine purchasing power parity (the rate of currency conversion that equalizes the purchasing power of different currencies by eliminating the differences in price levels between countries)
    • Berechnet nach der Kaufkraftparität, ist die Wirtschaftskraft mancher Schwellenländer deutlich höher als nominal angegeben. — Calculated according to purchasing power parity, the economic strength of some emerging markets is significantly higher than nominally stated.

    Synonyms: KKP, Kaufkraftausgleich

Etymology: Kauf (“purchase”) + Kraft (“power”) + Parität (“parity”)

column6:
noun
  1. masculine, strong cost-of-living allowance, purchasing power compensation (an additional payment to employees or pensioners to compensate for higher prices at a specific location or due to inflation)
    • Für die Entsendung nach Tokio gewährt das Unternehmen einen großzügigen Kaufkraftausgleich. — The company provides a generous cost-of-living allowance for the assignment to Tokyo.

    Synonyms: Teuerungszulage, Auslandszulage, Inflationsausgleich

Etymology: Kauf (“purchase”) + Kraft (“power”) + Ausgleich (“compensation/equalization”)

noun
  1. masculine, strong inflation compensation, cost-of-living adjustment (measures or payments intended to offset the effects of inflation on purchasing power)
    • Die Gewerkschaften fordern einen vollen Inflationsausgleich in der kommenden Tarifrunde. — The unions are demanding full inflation compensation in the upcoming collective bargaining round.

    Synonyms: Teuerungsausgleich, Reallohnsicherung

Etymology: Inflation (“inflation”) + Ausgleich (“compensation/balance”)

column4:
noun
  1. feminine wage-price spiral (a macroeconomic theory to explain the cause-and-effect relationship between rising wages and rising prices)
    • Um eine gefährliche Lohn-Preis-Spirale zu verhindern, mahnte die Zentralbank zu moderaten Tarifabschlüssen. — To prevent a dangerous wage-price spiral, the central bank urged moderate collective bargaining agreements.

    Synonyms: Zweitrundeneffekt, Kostendruckinflation

Etymology: Lohn (“wage”) + Preis (“price”) + Spirale (“spiral”)

noun
  1. feminine cost-of-living allowance, inflation bonus (a supplementary payment to compensate for rising prices of consumer goods)
